speechtext: That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act by authorizing the minister to make, with the approval of the governor in council, grants to universities supplementary to those by the act authorized, to assist in meeting the expenses incurred in training veterans.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: That it is expedient to present a measure to provide rights, privileges and benefits to and in respect of veterans of world war II domiciled in Canada at the time of joining the forces of allied nations, and to the widows and mothers of such veterans as died in service or subsequently but before they had received such rights, privileges and benefits in full.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: PENSION ACT AMENDMENT-ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for extended payments of pensions to veterans and their dependents as therein set out; to provide further for reorganization of the commission and for the salaries and duties of the chairman, deputy chairman and other members of the commission and generally to enlarge the scope and application of the act.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SPECIAL OPERATORS WAR SERVICE BENEFITS ACT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: That it is expedient to present a measure to make applicable, the allowances and benefits accorded to a veteran, to certain persons described as "special operators" who were enrolled in Canada by United Kingdom authorities for special duty during world war II, under the Veterans Land Act, 1942, the Veterans Insurance Act, the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, part I of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1946. the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, the Department of Veterans Affairs Act, the Civil Service Act, the Pension Act, the Income War Tax Act, the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, and the War Service Grants Act, 1944.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
That it is expedient to present a bill to make provision for the payment of allowances to or in respect of veterans of a prescribed age and veterans permanently unemployable or incapable of self maintenance through physical or mental disability and widows and orphan children of veterans. Provisions of the bill apply to veterans of the North West Rebellion, the South African war, world war I and world war II. Provision is made for establishing a war veterans' allowance board to administer the act and for the payment of the salaries of the members and pensions on retirement.

Veteran's Land Act

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: VETERANS BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS ACT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: That it is expedient to present a bill to authorize payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of losses, within the limitations therein provided, to banks incurred in respect of loans made to veterans resident and domiciled in Canada who have received or are entitled to receive a gratuity under the War Service Grants Act, 1944, and who have not elected to take benefits under the Veterans Land Act, 1942. Such loans to be confined to the purpose of establishing the veteran in business or professionally. Provision is also made for the payment of the necessary expenses of administration out of moneys appropriated by parliament.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, whereby provision is made, inter alia, that the Minister of Veterans Affairs may,
(a)	provide Canadian universities with moneys to enable them to make, as an emergency measure, small loans to veterans attending universities and also to pay expenses of repatriation of certain veterans discharged in the United Kingdom in order to take training outside of Canada and to pay transportation expenses of the wife and child of such veterans from the United Kingdom to Canada or other designated place outside of Canada;
(b)	provide training and re-training and pay allowances to a pensioner requiring such training by reason of an increase in his disabilities.
Provision is also made for entitlement of a member or former member of the Canadian forces to the statutory allowances and benefits in respect of all of his full-time service, if he is not accepted as a member of the permanent or regular_ force, or_ is not accepted for service for a special prescribed period; also for bringing a veteran suffering personal injury by accident when in training under the Government Employees Compensation Act.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: That it is expedient to amend the War Service Grants Act, 1944, to make provision inter alia (a) for the full payment of the statutory supplementary gratuity of a member who has joined the permanent naval or military forces or the regular air force or who has been accepted in the interim force, notwithstanding that he may have been required to accept pay and allowances at lower rates than were issuable to him or on his behalf immediately prior to the date of his joining the permanent or regular force or his acceptance in the interim force; (b) for a reestablishment credit for a member who does not elect to take benefits or training under the Veterans Land Act, 1942, or the Veterans Rehabilitation Act; (e) for a reestab-lisment credit to the widow or mother of a member who dies after discharge; (d) to permit a member to use his credit for the reduction or discharge of indebtedness on his home where he has already reduced such indebtedness.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: CIVILIAN WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES ACT

That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Veterans Land Act ,1942, to provide a change in the status of the director so as to integrate the administration of the Act more closely with other departmental activities administered by the minister and to provide authority for the director to contract with a veteran for the sale to him of land and improvements, building materials, and live stock and farm implements to a total cost to the director of five thousand eight hundred dollars upon the terms and conditions of payment therefor and in respect thereto contained in the said bill and regulations to be made thereunder.

Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): It was my intention, Mr. Chairman, with the consent of the committee-and only with that consent-to deal with all twelve measures in a short, concise statement. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With the unanimous consent of the committee, it is suggested that all the resolutions be considered, and that one motion be passed covering all of them.

speechtext: That is correct.

The agreement was on the understanding that when these bills came before the house on second reading there will be every opportunity for debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is quite correct.
With that understanding we are in agreement.
The same understanding exists in this group.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the house that I report these resolutions?
Veteran's Land Act
Was it not the minister's intention to make a statement at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I might have permission, Mr. Chairman, to give a concise, synoptic and factual statement of what the committee on veterans affairs has recommended, and what the government is prepared to accept, so that hon. members at second reading stage may have the opportunity of making such comments as they may deem advisable.
For the convenience of hon. members, and after consultation with other parties, I have decided to ask the indulgence of the committee in order that I may present in one concise, composite statement the entire programme of veterans' legislation. I have received the kind consent of the house, and having that consent, I purpose discussing the twelve measures with respect to which resolutions have been introduced. Eleven of these stand in my name, and one in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). With the kind indulgence of the house three of the resolutions have been moved forward this afternoon. These resolutions relate to the civilian war pensions and allowances bill and bills to amend the War Service Grants Act and the Veterans Land Act.
All twelve bills have been considered by the special select committee on veterans affairs. I wish at this point to pause to say that for thirty years I have been in parliament and have watched committees function. I want to pay a tribute-an entirely non-partisan tribute -to the finest committee of the House of Commons of Canada I have ever seen in action. That, sir, was the veterans affairs committee. We have had our contentions, and probably still have more of them; we have had our controversies; we have had occasional animader-sions; but I never saw a more devoted band of loyal gentlemen in my life. Indeed, if I were in charge of decorations and awards-which I am not

I would recommend them all for the Canada medal. They did a grand job-a wonderful job. We disagreed at times, of course. There were times when we did not go as far as some of my hon. friends, like the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), or the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) would like to have gone. But I think the work has been a wonderful work. The committee has written a veterans' charter for Canada, and for that work it will have the eternal gratitude of the veterans of this country. It will have the gratitude of a nation for the work it has done.
Ten of these bills have been recommended by the committee as such. With respect to
[The Chairman.l
two of them the committee has made recom- _ mendations; but the bills as introduced by the government are not completely in accord with the committee's recommendations.
These bills, and two which have preceded them, together with possibly one or two others standing in the name of other ministers, will be incorporated in the veterans' charter to be compiled. It is my intention to issue a vet-terans' charter, with the names of the sixty members of the committee on the front page, and to send it to every veterans' organization in the Dominion of Canada.
Five of the bills covered by the twelve resolutions to be discussed in this statement are amending bills. One is, in effect, an amending bill, but the amendments were so numerous that a completely new consolidation and revision is being presented.
Six of the bills are new legislation so far as this house is concerned. Four of the six new bills, however, deal with legislation which has already been in effect for some time by order in council under the War Measures Act. Nine of the twelve bills represent, to a substantial extent, the ratification by parliament of legislation enacted by order in council under the War Measures Act. Three of the bills are entirely new, and in almost all the bills, which are either amending bills or for the purpose of giving parliamentary sanction to orders in council, some new principles have been incorporated.
This body of legislation affects not only the veterans of world war II but the veterans of world war I, the veterans of the South African war and of the northwest rebellion. It affects Canadians who served in the forces of other members of the British commonwealth and in the forces of nations allied with His Majesty. Provision is made tfith respect to eleven different groups of persons who rendered loyal and hazardous service in world war II, although they were not formally enrolled in His Majesty's forces.
This statement will be exceedingly concise. I shall merely enumerate under the heading of each resolution or bill the principal enactments which are proposed without explanation or argument.
The first bill to which I shall refer is that covered by the resolution which I now move. It introduces a bill to amend the Pension Act. This bill with the one exception to which I shall refer later, is in exactly the terms recommended by the select committee. It consists of thirty-two sections and it affects all the veterans of any and every w'ar in which Canada has participated.

Veteran's Land Act
The principal features of the bill are as follows:
I.	The insurance principle, about which many of us have fought, including the hon. member for Vancouver South, which is restored.
At last.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
2. The benefits of the Canadian pension scale are extended to all Canadians who served in the forces of the British commonwealth or of allied nations.
3.	The pensions payable to dependent parents, in cases where a widow is also pensioned, are doubled.
4.	The salaries of the pension commissioners are increased.
5.	The duties of the veterans' bureau are expressly defined.
6.	The language defining non-pensionable preenlistment conditions has been restricted or narrowed, according to the particular interpretation put upon it.
7.	The period for which pension may be paid retroactively has been extended when delay in making the award has been due to conditions over which the applicant had no control.
8.	Pensioners entering hospital for treatment of their pensionable disabilities will receive their pensions during such periods of hospitalization.
9.	Blinded pensioners, on entering the department's institutions for custodial care, shall continue to receive the helplessness allowance by which pension in such cases is augmented.
10.	Widows who have obtained divorce or separation decrees from their pensioned husbands may when pensionable as widows be granted pension rates higher than the alimony awarded by the courts, at the discretion of the commission.
II.	Canadians who served in the ranks in the imperial forces during world war I are to receive the full benefits of the Canadian Pension Act as the act may have been amended subsequent to the agreement of 1920, by which the government of the United Kingdom agreed to pay to such veterans the Canadian scale.
12.	The principle of equal pensions for women, as for men, is adopted.
13.	The datelines of pension eligibility for wives, widows and children of world war I veterans have been advanced from 1930 and 1933, so that all wives married and children born prior to May 1, 1944, are included.
All the foregoing amendments were recommended by the select committee.
I want now to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). In addition, the government, in deference to opinions expressed by many members of the committee but mainly advocated by the hon. member, has broadened the provision regarding the eligibility of children. The bill provides that children born of marriages contracted prior to May 1, 1944, even though the birth is subsequent to that date, shall be eligible. I think my hon. friend was the one who advanced that before the committee.
Next is the war veterans' allowance bill. This measure, while essentially an amending enactment, takes the form of a completely new, revised and consolidated bill. It is for the most part a submission to parliament of amendments adopted during the war by order in council. The bill will come before the house exactly as recommended by the select committee. It covers the veterans of four wars, and it incorporates into the a/ct the widows' allowance measure approved by parliament in the appropriation act of 1943.
The bill is in three parts. Part I refers to veterans; part II refers to widows of veterans, and part III refers to what has formerly been known as the dual service pension.
The principal features of the bill which are new to this house are as follows:
1.	Women veterans are made eligible at the age of 55, the same as widows.
2.	It increases the basic allowances from $20 single and $40 married, to $30 and $60 respectively, thereby permitting the allowable income to be calculated on the higher figure. The small pensioner, eligible for the allowance, is thus permitted a materially improved standard of living. A single person may have a total income of $640. and a married person $1,130.
3.	Six items are added to the lists of types of income not deductible from allowances.
4.	The value of the veteran's home permissible without deduction from allowances is raised from $2,000 to $4,000.
5. Salaries of the commissioners	are increased.
6.	Several amendments have been made in the interests of children. First, step-children, adopted or foster-children are included within the definition of "child." Second, allowances may be paid with respect to children during their educational period up to the age of twenty-one years instead of nineteen as it is now. Third, allowances with respect to handicapped children may be paid beyond the age of twenty-one.
Veteran's Land, Act

The bill to amend the Veterans Land Act is exactly as recommended by the select committee. Its principal provisions are:
1.	Assistance may be given to tenant farmers, and to farmers holding land under agreement for sale.
2.	Former soldier settlers in default of their
contracts are permitted to qualify under the Veterans Land Act, if they have served in world war II.	[DOT]
3.	In conformity with the long established principles of responsible government, the minister is made responsible for administration of the act.
The next is the bill to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act. For reasons well known to the select committee, there are two bills amending this act. The first bill authorizes the government to make grants to universities, not exceeding $150 per student veteran, to enable the universities to provide the additional premises, equipment, staffs and services required to meet the extraordinary increase in enrolment, arising out of educational benefit provided for veterans under this act. The resolution covering this short bill was placed on the order paper, in advance of the other proposed amendments as an assurance to the universities that the government accepted responsibility for this proposal. Once the government had accepted the principle of the bill the universities felt justified in proceeding with their financial arrangements.
The second bill to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act contains a number of amendments which had not been fully dealt with by the select committee at the time the first bill was introduced. This second bill has now been recommended by the committee. Its principal provisions are:
1.	The government is authorized to advance money to universities, for the purpose of making loans to student veterans, under regulations. It is contemplated that loans shall not exceed $500 per year

or $2,000 in all. Applications will be dealt with by boards of senior faculty members with representation from the Department of Veterans Affairs.
2.	Veterans accepted for vocational training but not able to enter upon their training on account of lack of facilities or the necessity of conforming to entrance dates may receive out-of-work benefits while waiting, and the receipt of such benefit shall not count against the time for which benefits are otherwise available.
3.	The minister is granted power to make regulations regarding the extension of university training beyond a period equivalent to the length of the veteran's service.

4.	Recipients of educational and vocational training benefits shall not be eligible for the benefits of the Veterans Land Act, with certain minor exceptions in the case of agricultural training.
5.	Disabled pensioners who may acquire retraining as the result of their disabilities may receive such training at 'any time without sacrifice of their reestablishment credit.
6.	The periods of service upon which benefits under this act may be based and the dates at which service shall be deemed to have ended are specifically defined with respect to veterans who enter the interim or permanent forces. The definitions and cut-off dates are identical with those in the War Service Grants Act.
7.	Veterans in receipt of vocational training who may be injured as the result of such training shall be eligible for compensation under the Government Employees' Compensation Act.
Now I come to the bill to amend the War Service Grants Act. This bill is exactly as recommended by the select committee, except for a minor amendment to section 4. Its chief provisions are:
1.	Supplementary gratuity payable to a veteran who upon joining the permanent force reverts to a lower rank shall be calculated on the basis of the higher rank that he held before reverting.
2.	For the purpose of calculating gratuities and credit in the case of veterans who join the interim or permanent forces, the dates at which service counting towards gratuity shall be terminated are defined in the terms of an order in council promulgated early this year. The dates are the same as those in the bill to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.
3.	Widows and dependent mothers of veterans who die subsequent to discharge without having exercised all their reestablishment credit rights may receive the balance of the reestablishment credit to which the veteran was entitled.
4.	The uses to which reestablishment credit may be put are expanded in relation to the building of a house under the National Housing Act and in relating to the retirement of debt arising out of encumbrances on the veteran's house.
Now I come to a new piece of legislation that was recommended by the committee, the veterans business and professional loans bill. This is an entirely new piece of legislation. Its purpose is through a government guarantee to enable a veteran to borrow from a chartered bank a sum up to $3,000 at five per cent interest for the purpose of acquiring a busi-

Veteran's Land Act
ness, an interest- in a business, or the tools, implements or equipment of a trade, business or profession. The loans depart from ordinary bank practice id the Bank Act in that: (a) the maximum interest is fixed at five per cent; (b) the taking of security on land is authorized; (c) the period for repayment may be extended to ten years. Loans may not exceed two-thirds of the expenditure upon the purpose for which the loan is granted. The maximum of loans subject to the guarantee is 825,000,000. The guarantee is in the form of a blanket guarantee to each individual bank, at the rate of twenty-five per cent of any loss incurred on the first million dollars lent by such bank, and at the rate of fifteen per cent on loans in excess of one million dollars by any bank.
Next is the supervisors war service benefits bill. This bill has not been specifically recommended by the select committee. It was considered by the committee, which recommended that supervisors be granted exactly the same rights as former members of the forces. The bill provides that they shall be with respect to their overseas service on a par with former members of the forces with the single exception of income tax exemption. The subject. of income tax has already been debated in this house on the .budget resolutions.
I come next to the fire fighters war service benefits bill. This bill has not been recommended by the select committee. The committee made a recommendation that members of the Corps of (Civilian) Canadian Fire Fighters for Service in the United Kingdom should receive the same rehabilitation benefits as former members of the armed forces. The government did not concur fully in this recommendation. The bill confirms the following benefits already granted by order in council: Gratuity on the same basis as veterans with regard to overseas service; rehabilitation grant; the Veterans Land Act with respect to pensioners. Additional to the benefits conferred by order in council the bill will grant all former members of the corps who served overseas the right to vocational training, and will allow their overseas time to be calculated under the Unemployment Insurance Act the same as for veterans.
Next is the civilian war pensions and allowances bill. This bill substantially represents the recommendation of the select committee but with slight variations, which will be explained as I proceed. Its purpose is to confer the right- to pension upon certain groups of persons who rendered valiant service in the war but who were not attested as
members of His Majesty's forces. With respect to the following groups, the bill is in the terms recommended by the select committee:
1.	Merchant seamen.
2.	Commercial fishermen.
3.	Auxiliary services personnel.
4.	Canadian overseas fire fighters.
5.	Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
6.	R.C.MjP.-Special constable guards.
7.	Air raid precautions workers. .
S.	Potential recruits sustaining disability while undergoing treatment in the care of the Department of Veterans Affairs for the purpose of removing disabilities which debarred them from enlistment.
The draft bill as recommended by the select committee included also civil government employees incurring death or disability as the result of enemy action or counter-action. Upon consideration the government was not satisfied that this was the appropriate method of providing for the pension rights of these government employees, and this group is not included in the bill. The opportunity for further consideration of the most appropriate method of providing for this group is desired by the government. I can assure the house, however, that this does not result from any desire or intent to diminish in any way the rights which civil government employees acquired under the order in council which provided for their pension entitlement. The government has been assured by its legal advisers that no rights already conferred will be lost as the result of deferring legislative action with regard to them. All the civilian groups to which I have already referred were covered by order in council, and the parts of the bill recommended by the select committee referring to these groups follow the terms of the orders in council with exceedingly minor variations.
The select committee also recommended that five other groups be accorded pension rights in this bill, but did not pass upon the actual terms of the legislation now to be introduced with respect to those groups.
One group recommended by the committee has not been accepted by the government, and is not included in the bill. This group consists of former members of the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers. No claims have arisen from members of this organization and it would seem unnecessary, therefore, to include them in the bill at this time.
The four groups included in the bill upon the committee's recommendation, but with
Income War Tax

respect to whom the committee did not have the opportunity of passing upon the precise terms of the legislation, are as follows:
1.	Members of the voluntary aid detachment serving with the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps in Canada.
2.	Overseas welfare workers, which include those who, under the auspices of the Canadian Red Cross Society or the Saint John Ambulance Brigade, left Canada to serve overseas as welfare workers, nursing aides, ambulaiiee or transport drivers, members of the overseas headquarters staff, or in any other capacity.
3.	Orthopaedic nurses selected by the Canadian Red Cross Society for service overseas with the Scottish ministry of health.
4.	Canadian civilian air crew of the Royal Air Force Transport Command.
The government's proposal in the bill to follow the resolution is that members of the voluntary aid detachment shall be pensionable on the same terms as members of the air raid precautions organization. The scale of pensions for these two groups corresponds closely with the rates payable under workmen's compensation.
Overseas welfare workers and orthopaedic nurses are granted their eligibility for pension on approximately the same terms as merchant seamen.
The civilian air crew personnel of the Royal Air Force Transport Command are granted their entitlement on a basis of need upon very much the same principle as was applicable under the former section 11 (3) of the Pension Act.
Now I come to the special operators war service benefits bill. This bill is exactly as recommended by the select committee. I think the house knows who these special operators were-about seventy men who were taken by External Affairs and who flew over and descended by parachute into enemy areas during the war and did magnificent service. The purpose of the bill is to confer all rehabilitation, pension and other veteran legislation upon these men. There are three others who served in other theatres of war, and they also will be looked after in regard to these benefits.
I understood there might be some others besides these three.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It will not be limited to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The last one is the allied veterans benefits 'bill. This bill is exactly as recommended by the select committee. It affects Canadians who served in

the allied forces in the event of their returning to Canada, and their dependents domiciled and resident in Canada. The bill is designed to ratify an order in council passed early this year on recommendation of the select committee on veterans affairs which sat in the autumn of 1945, and goes a little further. By the order in council and by the bill, Canadians who served in the allied forces upon returning to Canada, are eligible under: the Veterans Rehabilitation Act; the Veterans Land Act; the War Service Grants Act; and the Department of Veterans Affairs Act.
Owing to the fact that members of the forces of certain of our allies were, in effect, discharged in 1940 when Germany overran the low countries and France, the language of the bill has been sufficiently broadened in comparison with the order in council to ensure that Canadians in the forces of those countries shall not be excluded by reason of the fact that they were unable to return to Canada within two years of their discharge.
In conformity with the War Service Grants Act, widows and dependent mothers are made eligible to receive gratuities and reestablishment credit under the same conditions as the similar dependents of former members of the Canadian forces. The bill provides that any similar benefits received from the country in whose forces beneficiaries under the bill may have served shall be deducted from the Canadian benefits.
I wish to conclude by saying that we shall have our differences in debate in regard to some of these matters, but no committee of the House of Commons ever did a finer job than the veterans affairs committee of 1946. May I say in regard to my colleague and parliamentary assistant that no committee ever had a finer or abler or keener chairman than the hon. member for Rosthern, and even if he be conscripted or bludgeoned into other duties in a far-away province in the near future the veterans of Canada will never forget and the country will always gratefully remember, the work that he has done on their behalf.

speechtext:
The committee is on
resolution 12.

I did not intend to speajc at any length on taxation of cooperatives, either on the budget or on the present resolution. The reason is that three members of our group before becoming members of the House of Commons were for a great many years members of cooperatives. On the budget resolution, and also on the budget itself, they dealt very ably with this matter, and laid the views of this group before the House of Commons. I do not want to take up too much time in discussing the matter this afternoon, but because I have had a great deal of correspondence in the matter from my own riding, I thought I ought to put myself on record.
As I understand it, the cooperatives throughout this country object to the government's taxation proposals on five main grounds. Just before the house rose last session, I believe it was December 18, the royal commission which investigated this question made its report. That report was studied by practically every cooperative throughout this country, and between the first of January and the first of June of this year they communicated with every member of this house urging them to oppose the taxation of cooperatives. Personally I had about thirty-eight resolutions from different cooperatives in Manitoba urging me to oppose this taxation. When the government brought down its budget proposals, particularly the present resolution, a large number of our members and, I suppose, members of other parties as well, received telegrams and registered letters from various cooperatives urging that we ask the government to reconsider some of their suggestions with respect to taxation and, if possible, to discontinue entirely the proposal for taxation of cooperatives.
I was particularly interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Cariboo with respect to this situation. I think he judged the matter rightly when he stated the purpose of the royal commission which investigated this problem some time ago was not to find out if cooperatives should be taxed, but how it would be possible to apply taxation to the cooperatives. I think that is a true statement of the situation.
Income War Tax

In the communications I have had on the matter, cooperatives in my district and elsewhere in Manitoba are worried because the government ignores the basic difference between a cooperative business and a private business. They contend that we fail to recognize the difference between business done on a cooperative basis and business done on an individual basis.
Their second objection is this. Cooperatives are treated, according to government legislation, as private businesses. The government's resolution forces cooperatives to treat members and non-members on the same basis. Non-members are entitled under resolution 12 to patronage dividends.
Third, this legislation prevents cooperatives from providing service at cost by forcing them to pay taxes on not less than three per .cent of the employed capital. I think that should come in for a little discussion at this time. I presume that means three per cent of the capital employed in the business. There is one question which I should like to ask the minister. Does that mean that the remainder of the revenue of the cooperative is to be distributed as patronage dividends? Suppose a cooperative decides by a vote of its membership to use, we will say, sixty per cent of its income for the expansion of its business; will that sixty per cent be subject to tax under the Income War Tax Act or under the corporation tax act, in the amount, I believe, of about thirty per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would if it were retained in the company for expansion of business. If it were declared as a patronage dividend, and if the member lent it back to the cooperative, no question of taxation would be involved. The essence of it is that a cooperative no more than anyone else can build up capital out of tax-exempt income, in the proper sense of income.

I am glad to have that statement from the minister, because a great many cooperatives have been extremely worried as to what the government's policy would be in that regard. The fourth matter is this-interference with the right of the individual member to leave savings with the cooperative for the provision of further service by forcing payment of cash within six months. That has been extended to one year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. That point is cleared up. There is no interference. The individual member is perfectly free to leave the whole or a portion of his patronage dividend with the cooperative if he wishes to do so.

Would it not be taxed at three per cent? The fifth question is with

respect to retroactive taxation, and I take it that refers largely to the wheat pool. I know it is the wheat pools in my riding that are particularly concerned about retroactive taxation. I submit that for two reasons there should not be retroactive taxation. First, it would be a reversal of the policy declared by the Minister of Finance when section 4 p was enacted, and secondly, cooperators generally relied upon section 4p as granting them exemption under the Income War Tax Act. In the opinion of the royal commission they were justified in that reliance. Secondly, it would be a reversal of the attitude of the administrative officials for years. WThen the department changed its attitude, cooperatives were placed in a position of uncertainty which has continued to this time. Until the uncertainty is removed, cooperatives are at a loss to know how to conduct their operations in compliance with section 4 p.
From what paper has the hon. gentleman been reading?

I have been referring to an
article appearing in the Manitoba Cooperator with reference to the first two paragraphs of section 4p of the Income War Tax Act. The wheat pools in Manitoba are particularly concerned about this matter: The set-up of the wheat pools in that province is somewhat different from that in Saskatchewan and Alberta, as I understand it. The pools in Manitoba are operated on a community basis, so to speak, in that the pool belongs to the individual community in which it is located. Since 1942 and 1943 there has been a fear that they would be subject to taxation. The result is that the wheat pools, in Manitoba, particularly, are not certain what their position is with respect to taxation, and they have urged that the whole matter be reconsidered by the government.
There is something else to which the attention of the government should be directed. It is not only the fishermen and farmers that are opposed to the present taxation of cooperatives. I have an interesting letter from the Manitoba trades and labour council dated June 11, 1946. It is a long letter and I am not going to quote it, but I think I ought to give the substance of its opinions. All other members from Manitoba have received this same letter. The trades and labour council goes on record as urging the government to desist from applying taxation to the cooperatives throughout the country, and they also go on record as opposing the taxation of cooperative organizations.

Income War Tax
There is only one other item that should be dealt with at this time. Up to the present a great many members have spoken on this subject and, I presume each individual member has been speaking for himself. I think the leaders of all groups should go on record as speaking for their respective parties so far as taxation of cooperatives is concerned. This is too important a matter to be discussed on an individual basis, and I do not think that because one member gets up and speaks in the first person singular he should be regarded as speaking for his party. Every party should go on record and tell the country where it stands with respect to the taxation of cooperatives.

Having listened to the discussion of the resolution during three or four sittings of the committee I am still debating in my own mind whether I should reserve my comments for the second reading and committee stages of the bills, or present them on this resolution. In any event I feel I should say a word or two at this point.
I rise chiefly to register my opposition to the remaining two or three objectionable features of this resolution respecting the proposed taxation of cooperatives. Although the Acting Minister of Finance has proposed three minor amendments which remove some of the objectionable provisions of the resolution as it was originally proposed, it appears to me that the most objectionable feature remains. I have in mind the adoption of the principle of imposing taxation on a true and genuine cooperative. I am not so much concerned about the amount of the tax or the rates of taxation; it is the principle that matters.
The minister said that if capital produces a reasonable return it should be taxed. But suppose the capital of a cooperative is made up entirely of the benefits which accrue from business which has been done strictly among the members of the cooperative, and who were in the first place taxed when they received their earnings and of course paid the tax. I should be inclined to think that if the members of a cooperative desire to purchase their requirements through their own cooperative organization in order that their dollars may be stretched as far as possible they should not be taxed on the money which they have saved in buying goods cooperatively, after they have already paid tax on their original earnings.
In the discussion that took place the other day the acting minister did not fully explain the revolving fund, even though hon. members came back to it more than once. I should like to have an explanation. In fact, the minister has made two statements which 63260-256
seem to me to be contradictory in answer to questions by the member for Acadia and the leader of the Social Credit group, the member for Peace River. At page 3945 of Hansard the following appears:
Mr. Quelch:	Are we to understand that if
a certain amount is paid out of the revolving fund and a certain amount of new capital is put in. that new capital will be taxable?
Mr. Abbott: Not unless it increases the fund.
Mr. Quelch:	Then it will not be possible to
expand the business without paying the tax?
Mr. Abbott:	That is right.
At page 3950 of Hansard the hon. member for Peace River said:
Is there not just one limitation to what the minister has just said in connection with the $25 which is kept by the cooperative on behalf of a member-
Mr. Abbott:	And on his instructions.
Mr. Low:	Yes. If that results in a net increase in the revolving fund, does not that become taxable?
Mr. Abbott:	No. I realize that it is a little
confusing, but the answer is definitely, no.
I wonder which of these answers is the correct one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Both statements are perfectly correct-no contradiction.
I still need some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the rest of my statement on page 3950 he will see that I made a further explanation of the revolving fund.

At any rate it appears to me that even if the cooperatives do business strictly with their own members they will still have to pay taxes, provided that they have an income which is taxable. I personally object to the introduction of the principle of the taxation of cooperatives. I concur in the proposition that in fairness to other forms of business, earnings derived from business done with non-members should be taxed.
Speaking on this resolution on July 26 the hon. member for Cariboo in effect said that he would not worry very much if private enterprise were to go out of business. On the other hand there are those in the income tax association who would like to see the cooperatives go out of business. Personally I cannot subscribe to either. of these views. I am in favour of both private business and cooperative business. The cooperative type of business and private business are necessary in the economy of a democratic country. Perhaps that is the line which the group to which I belong can draw in contrast to the stand taken on this matter by our friends to our immediate right. When cooperatives do business with their own members who have paid personal

Income War Tax

income tax on their earnings they should not be taxed. When people get together and decide on buying goods and services in a cooperative way they should not be taxed a second time. They have paid their tax on their original earnings, and if they choose to stretch their dollars as far as possible, why should they not do it? W'hy should they then be taxed a second time on these earnings, or on the saving which acrues and which makes up the lump sum which may be called capital, and which, as the minister says, will be subject to taxation under the proposed legislation?
I received twenty telegrams from cooperatives representing several hundred members, and also fourteen letters, protesting against the taxation of cooperatives. I also received 271 cards asking me to support the taxation of cooperatives. It is therefore obvious that there are two different views on this matter. Personally I should like to be fair to these two groups, and I should like to see justice done to both private enterprise and to cooperative business. A man who goes into private business and renders to ithe people a good service should have the opportunity of expanding and continuing his business and further rendering this service. On the other hand, if a group of individuals choose to get together and buy cooperatively in order to remedy their lack of purchasing power, they should have the privilege of buying cooperatively in bulk, perhaps saving a little bit, and at the same time stretching every dollar as far as possible. Once we introduce legislation adopting the principle of taxation on cooperatives I am afraid that if the government decides to raise taxes in the future all it will have to do will be to present the legislation to the house and we shall have higher taxation on cooperatives. On behalf of the people I represent I object to the taxation of genuine cooperatives. I know it is difficult to define what is a cooperative, but the government should present legislation defining cooperatives and at the same time should introduce a cooperative act within the four corners of which all the cooperatives could fall.
That is all I wish to say at this stage. If I have any further remarks to make I believe they can be best made when the bills are presented.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
During the morning debate there was a great deal of discussion on the three per cent provision of the resolution, and perhaps some confusion. It seemed to me that much of the misunderstanding may be due to a misunderstanding of accounting principles and practice rather than to provisions

of the law. It may be that all my answers were not strictly accurate, although I believe they were substantially correct.
I think the situation can best be described in this way. If no legislation were to be enacted respecting the tax status of patronage dividends, cooperatives would be taxable on their income as determined under the Income War Tax Act. In some cases, as I have pointed out, they would have no taxable income. In other cases, cooperatives and ordinary companies would find themselves subject to taxes hnd would be unable under the ordinary law to deduct patronage dividends as an expense. For example, according to the law officers of the crown the whea.t pools would be unable to deduct patronage dividends as an expense of doing business. The proposed legislation, therefore, enables a cooperative or any other company to pay patronage dividends out of income that would otherwise be taxable under the Income War Tax Act, and to deduct such patronage dividends before paying tax. The only limitation is that they shall not be able to distribute their income in the form of tax-free patronage dividends to such a point as to reduce their taxable income below three per cent on capital employed, as set out in the resolution.
In order to illustrate the reasons for the three per cent limitation, I am going to compare the relative positions of two cooperatives, alike in all other respects except that one cooperative has financed itself with the issuance of share capital on which it pays a limited dividend, and the other has financed itself on a revolving fund basis, no interest being paid on patronage dividends declared but not paid.
Taking cooperative A, with a capital of $50,000, represented by shares on which a limited dividend of 4 per cent is paid; it has a surplus in a given year of $5,000. Ordinary dividends to shareholder members amount to $2,000, and patronage dividends $3,000, making up a total of $5,000.
We then take cooperative B, with a similar capital of $50,000, which is represented by a revolving fund on which no interest is paid. There is the same surplus of $5,000, with no dividends or interest paid. Patronage dividends amount to $5,000.
If there were no three per cent rule, cooperative A-the first one I mentioned-which financed with share capital would pay tax on $2,000, whereas cooperative B, which earned exactly the same amount but which financed on a revolving fund, would pay no tax. Yet the only difference between the two organizations is in their method of financing. The

Income War Tax
members are the same, and the surplus is the same. The three per cent rule, as the committee will appreciate, corrects that discrimination to some extent, although not entirely.

I wish to correct one point of view expressed by the hon. member of Vegre-ville. I have no disagreement with his expressing his own view, but he did say I had expressed the view that there was no room for private business. His justification for saying that arose from an interchange between the acting minister and myself during the course of my remarks on the subject. The point under discussion at that time was that if a private corporation requires legislation of this kind for the taxation of cooperatives in order that that corporation may exist, then we can do without it.
Let us look at the recommendation of the commission in this respect. It says that the object is to make certain that the solution finally adopted will not ruin one or the other. Apparently the only way to prevent the ruination of private business in certain communities is by putting on a tax such as that to which my hon. friend has just objected. I say if that is the only way to save them, then they ought to be ruined. That was my view.
I do not say there is no room for private business. If a community wishes to pay a private business a profit for doing their business for them, that is a matter for them. But if another community wants to do its own business and to save its profit for itself, so that it will not be paid out to any other person, then I say it should not be compelled to keep alive in that community an organization which can exist only by taking profit or toll from that community, and to do it at the expense of the cooperative. That is very different from saying that I want to wipe out all private business. There may be room at any time under any system for a certain amount of private business. But I am saying that that private business must not be permitted to exist by imposing a restriction upon a cooperative. That was the argument of the commission, and the argument I used in my interchange with the minister.

I do not wish to be unfair to the hon. member, or to place upon his words an interpretation different from what he had in mind. For that reason I should like to place on record the exact words of the hon. member for Cariboo as they are recorded at page 3938 of Hansard:
So what the minister regards as fairness is to try to prevent the cooperatives from entirely swallowing up private business.
Mr. Abbott:	Why not?

if it is not functioning in the best interests of the common people? If it cannot stand up and carry out its own philosophy in competing with cooperatives, it ought to go out of business.
Mr. Abbott:	Compete on fair terms, yes.
I am afraid that in this regard I am inclined to support the minister's view, even though I have expressed the view, and still do, that cooperatives should not be taxed. But when it comes to private business I believe it would be well for hon. members to State definitely whether they do or do not support private enterprise, because we must recognize that private enterprise also plays an important part in the economy of the nation.
In recent months and years we have heard a great, deal against private enterprise. I accept the hon. member's statement as to what he had in mind, but I suggest that all groups should definitely express themselves as to whether they are supporting private enterprise and its expansion, while at the same time wishing to see cooperatives expand.

I do not believe it would be possible for a private corporation successfully to compete with a true cooperative in the same community, unless this parliament or government gave some privilege to the private corporation.
They are competing in the matter of management. That is all they need.

They will not be able to do
even that, because we have developed and are still developing some able management in cooperatives. While I am on my feet I would add that we have to make up our minds whether we are going to bolster up certain things which have outlived their usefulness at the expense of new developments, in order to try to balance them. That is the principle stated by the commission, namely that of making certain that the solution finally adopted would not ruin one or the other. Well, if the day were afraid of the night and the night were afraid of the day, and this government were to pass legislation to keep them balanced, we should have perpetual and eternal twilight, with neither day nor night.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is expecting too much, even of this government.

I am not charging the government with trying deliberately to destroy cooperatives. I know the Minister of Finance is one of the most sincere, diligent and competent members of the government. I would not suggest he had any such thing in mind. And I would even add that the acting minister is not far from the same calibre of man.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Damning with faint praise.

But I do say the government is ill-advised in following the recommendations of those who are in direct competition with cooperatives and who find that the cooperative method is making it difficult for them to carry on. As I have said, the reason it is difficult is just this: A community through its cooperative would have no profits, but the savings made from the cooperative effort remain as savings instead of going to a private corporation to help to make up its profits. That is exactly the situation, and the legislation which the government is now discussing is of such a type as to leave no line of demarcation between the private corporation and the cooperative. In other words, it is a hypodermic injection of capitalistic virus beneath the skin of the cooperative.

I should like to place before the committee my view with regard to the taxation of cooperatives. It has been contended by the grain exchange and by others who wish to have cooperatives taxed that there is no difference between the line elevators and the cooperatives, since they both handle grain under the Canada Grain Act. But as a cooperator for over thirty years I know there is a fundamental difference. The line elevator companies are in business for one purpose only. They are not set up to do missionary work among the farmers, but rather to make money as joint stock companies-to make all the tariff will bear, all the time. When new railroads were built through the west, and even before the steel reached the different points, there was a frantic rush by line elevator companies to acquire elevator sites; and what a wonderfully remunerative business it was! The line elevators had five shovels which they stuck into every load of grain, namely, weight, grade, dockage, price spreads and service and handling charges.
In connection with weights, it was a common practice to show 200 pounds less on the grain ticket than was recorded on the beam of the scale. As to grades, a man had to take any grade that was offered, the standard excuse being that there was room only for No. 3. The spreads were between three and five cents between Nos. 1 and 2 northern-and I am talking now about 1915, 1916 and 1920, before the cooperative elevators started, and 1923, before the pools started. As I say, there was a difference of from three to five cents between No. 1 and No. 2 northern, from five to seven cents between grades 2 and 3, and from six to eight cents between grades 3 and 4. The wheat board spreads to-day are just about half of that. In many instances there was a loss of

15 to 20 cents a bushel between wagon load and car load lots. This was discrimination against the small farmer, the man with the wagon load, in favour of the man who could sell in car load lots. The pool put street wheat or wagon loads on the same basis as car load lots.
What about the United Grain Growers; did they not have a considerable effect on that?

Possibly at one time, but in later years they stayed pretty close to their friends the grain exchange and refused to go into the pool. The hon. gentleman knows that.
In the matter of dockage it was a common thing to lose two bushels in excess dockage on a 75 bushel load by the policy adopted by the trade. Because of that method literally hundreds of thousands of bushels were sold by the trade for which the farmer never got credit on his statement.
The pools have reduced service and handling charges by about one-half. All this saving goes into the price the farmer receives for his grain and constitutes a part of his income. It was such abuses as these that forced the farmers to form cooperatives, to come together to do things for themselves. I personally went, through all the experiences I have related. I found that when I took exception to those abuses, changing elevators did not help any. The farther down the line I went, the tougher it got. I was a rebel. As I say, the difference between the line elevators and the pool elevators is that the line elevators are in business to make money, while the farmers in a cooperative elevator know that they are going to get service and save money for themselves. Farmers grouped themselves together in a cooperative in order to save money.
In my view the pool elevator is nothing more or less than an Extension of the granary on the farm. I joined in building a pool elevator in order to save myself from exploitation-just plain stealing. The money saved by the cooperative method of handling grain is directly a part of the farmer's income. Just as I went into the modern mechanized farming to cut costs so I went into the modern cooperative methods in order to help myself and eliminate excess service and handling charges.
My returns from the cooperative are not based on my share capital, as in line elevator joint stock companies. In the cooperative, one share means one vote. If I did not deliver any grain to the cooperative, my one share would not increase in value, and I would not receive any share in the earnings of the cooperative. Anything over and above the actual cost of

Income War Tax.
handling the grain is either returned to me in the form of excess handling charges, or is used as a reserve to carry on the business or to take care of liabilities, in proportion to my contribution of grain. In either case it would be credited to me as a member. There are 127,000 members who are direct owners of the cooperative wheat producers. As individuals they are liable to income tax on earnings saved, but the cooperative as a whole should not be subject to taxation.
The Saskatchewan Cooperative Wheat Producers now receive over fifty per cent of all the grain delivered to country elevators in Saskatchewan. This is the real cause of the fight. The heyday of the private grain trade is over, because the farmers have learned the hard way. They know what the so-called "farmer's friends" have done in the past and they know what they would do in the future if they get the chance. The grain trade's last bet is to call upon the government to cripple the cooperatives by taxation. Surely, Mr. Chairman, an institution like the wheat pools ivhieh have to borrow from $45,000,000 to $50,000,000 must have some reserves. They must put up at least fifteen per cent of their own money in order to get credit. In a year like 1937, with little wheat to handle, the pools kept their elevators open to distribute relief, and provided a great service to rural municipalities. Their deficit was nearly $2,000,000. It was a service that was helpful to the government, because it provided people with the means to live, and kept them off the relief rolls. The line elevators were mostly shut down at that time. We found out then who the government's friends *were, who the farmers' friends were and who the country's friends were.
In my opinion a cooperative democracy is the only solution to avert the fast approaching crisis within our capitalist economy. If the government is going to take sides with the people who want to see the cooperatives taxed and crippled and put out of business, then I say the war is on. The British people had the good sense to see the handwriting on the wall. I hope that this government will sit up and take notice.
The Progressive Conservative members to my right have said that the Liberal government is going socialist. I think it can be honestly said that any steps which the Liberal government has taken towards socialism have been brought about by the pressure of sheer cold necessity. I am very glad that the government has had the good judgment to have this whole question of taxation of cooperatives
looked into, and I hope that the minister will continue to exercise his good judgment in the interests of equity, justice and liberty.
I have had a number of telegrams and letters which I shall not read, because many of them have been put on the record a number of times, but I would strongly urge the government to place a truly dominion cooperative act on the statute books, and then we shall know where we are going and what we are doing.

I have two or three questions to ask the minister, but before doing so I want to go on record as whole-heartedly supporting the stand taken by other members of this group in opposing completely any taxation of cooperatives apart from the business which they might do with non-members. It has been said by others in this group that there is something more involved in the taxation of cooperatives than the loss of funds to the government, because within the cooperative movement there is an opportunity for people of all political and religious faiths and of various racial origins to meet on a common plane and work out their problems together.
I have received a number of communications from cooperatives in my constituency, and one which I was exceedingly pleased to get was from Mr. Eugene Bachelu, of LaFleche, president of the French-Canadian cooperative associations of Saskatchewan. Mr. Bachelu is also secretary of the LaFleche Cooperative Association, which is composed of both French and English-speaking Canadians.
There are one or two questions I would ask the minister which have not, I think, been asked at least in this way before. Does the minister believe that any government measure should reflect the desires of the majority of the electors?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will answer that in the affirmative.
The minister says yes. Then I would ask the minister if he believes that that the majority of Canadians support the present measure for the taxation of cooperatives.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would think so.
I disagree with the minister. I do not think it is possible for him to show definitely that the majority of Canadians support the taxation of cooperatives.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No more than it is possible for my hon. friend to show that they do not.

I will wager that I can make a better job of showing that the majority of
Income War Tax

the people who have spoken on this question do not support the government's position, than the minister can do to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The majority of persons who have spoken on it come from the group of which my hon. friend is a member.

But there has been discussion of it elsewhere than in this house. I was in touch with various labour organizations and was informed that they have gone on record as supporting the cooperative movement and have asked their members to study and support it. I have a resolution here passed by the Ontario federation of labour, in convention February 10-11, 1945, representing 150,000 workers. The resolution unanimously opposed the taxation of cooperatives and credit unions. That is the voice of organized labour in Ontario. There is a total of 600,000 organized workers in Canada.
I have also a booklet from the Cooperative Union of Canada in which it is stated that at least three-quarters of a million members in their cooperative union or in cooperative associations are affiliated with the Cooperative Union of Canada. There you have the voice of 750,000 people supporting the cooperative movement, as well as the opinion of a large proportion of the working classes who are organized in labour unions. I say to the minister and to the government that if any government measure falls in line with the opinions of organized labour and of the organized farmers, he can take a chance on it that it is in the interest of Canadians generally. I would also say this, that when the government brings in a measure that is opposed by organized labour and the organized farmers through their cooperatives, it is a measure which in my opinion does not represent the opinion of the majority of Canadians.
I would ask the minister another question. Does he believe that any taxation by a government should be based on the principle or belief that the moneys derived from the tax can foe better spent for the welfare of the population as a whole in the hands of the government than if left in the hands of the taxpayer? .

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is a long and involved question, but I will answer it in this way. I believe that any system of taxation should be fair as between Canadians, and if a Canadian doing one type of business should pay his share of a tax, a Canadian doing the same type of business in another way should pay his share of the tax. I agree with the commission's statement-I have not the statement
[Mr. Argue.l
before me, but it is to the effect that fiscal measures are a poor way of assisting a particular type or method of carrying on business.

I do not think any taxation proposals can fit equitably private enterprise and cooperatives, because they are diametrically opposed; they have different objectives. If it is to be taxation based upon the same formula it will not meet the interests of the majority of Canadians. I do not know, and the minister says in answer to another question he does not know, how much money is likely to come to the coffers of the government through this taxation proposal. It may be a million dollars, it may be two or three million dollars; I do not know. But I suggest to the government, while recognizing the need for government institutions to have money, that that one, or two or three million dollars would benefit Canadians generally much more if it were left in the hands of the patrons of cooperatives rather than taken into the government treasury. A cooperative oil refinery was set up in Saskatchewan a little more than ten years ago. Within a few years the price of gasoline, not only to members of that cooperative but to non-members, to all the people within that area, went down from six to eight cents a gallon. The amount of money invested in that refinery at that time was less than a million dollars, and I suggest that the consumers in that area with that million dollars were able to do something which was of greater benefit to the people of that area than if that money or any part of it had gone to the federal treasury. So I believe that, as cooperatives are able to expand throughout Canada, at least during the time when they are combating and overcoming monopolistic interests it is to the benefit of the people that the cooperatives should have all the money possible left with them so that they can complete the job they have undertaken.
We had a long debate in parliament on the 12J per cent increase in farm machinery. The members of our group thought at that time, and still think, that that increase was not justified. But if we had had a cooperative movement for the production and distribution of agricultural machinery we would not have needed to concern ourselves with the question whether the competitors of the cooperative farm machinery companies were able to increase their prices or not, because the people who saw fit to support and patronize their own cooperative would receive their farm machinery at cost.
We debated, too, this session the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. Those amendments, it is hoped, will allow the government to deal more successfully with

Income War Tax
the problem of monopoly and enable it better to break up existing combines. I believe it is a much wiser procedure not to tax any part of the savings of cooperatives but rather to encourage and if necessary sponsor them, because cooperatives are the best assurance in the world that combines will be broken and that they shall not be formed in future to the detriment of Canadians.
A good deal of consideration was given by this government to the problem we are likely to be faced with in another two, three or four years in the way of unemployment, depression and deflation. I was sorry to hear that the government, at least for the time being, has abandoned its social security and its public investment programmes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend is covering the waterfront here, with cartels and unemployment programmes. I hope he will stick as closely as possible to the terms of the resolution.

I thank the minister for his interjection. I was just going on to say that cooperatives are the instrument that prevents deflation, and when we are considering the taxation of cooperatives we must consider them in relation to the whole Canadian economy and determine how their growth will react upon the economy generally. The government, according to their own submission, believe that at some time public investment may be necessary. An ordinary corporation at various times has surpluses, which it may decide to distribute as dividends. Often the people who receive those dividends are not in the low income brackets but possess high incomes and do not feel the need of spending that money. Other profits of corporations may be retained as reserves, undistributed reserves, and reserves not used for capital expansion or for the increasing of inventories. That does not apply to cooperatives. If a cooperative retains within the cooperative association part of the savings it has made, it uses it for expansion, and because it spends, employment is provided. If the cooperative does not retain the money, it then pays it out as patronage dividends, and that money in the hands of low income earners is spent and goes into circulation and provides employment. When the government is considering taxation of cooperatives it should not consider it merely from the point of view of what advantage cooperatives may or may not have now as compared with private enterprise, but rather it should consider the whole cooperative movement in Canada, how it affects Canadians at this time and how its growth and expansion may be used to better economic conditions in this country. I suggest to the government that if it wants to do in respect of cooperatives that which is in the best interests of Canadians generally, now and in the future, it will totally abandon any proposals it now has for the taxation of cooperatives.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: To some extent.

To some extent, yes. As I sat listening to that, my mind roamed over the debates we have had in this house for a long time; I remembered how on occasion I have sat here, as my colleagues have done, and we have had thrown at us the accusation that we believe in compulsion. Of course that is quite untrue; but if ever there was a case of the compulsion of a group of people, here we have one. We have a group of people who organize a cooperative society, public-spirited citizens who say that, for the benefit of themselves and of the institution they are going to build, any funds they put into the capital of the cooperative association shall be contributed freely and without interest for the entire group. We now have legislation which says that before a patronage dividend can be paid by the people who comprise that group they must first of all compute three per cent interest on the capital, employed. In other words, we are compelling a group of people to do something which they themselves do not wish to do because they believe it is against the best interests of the organization they are establishing.
As I interjected on the night the budget was introduced, I believe that this provision in the budget in regard to cooperatives is fundamental. We have had a great deal of discussion of patronage dividends; we have had a great deal of discussion of other phases of the government's proposals; and may I say that I am thoroughly in accord with my colleagues who have placed the point of view of this party before the house in this long debate. But if there is one feature of the proposals which, in my opinion, is bad from the point of view of cooperatives, it is this three per cent feature. It strikes at the very basis of the cooperative movement.
Income War Tax

I do not think this has perhaps occurred to the minister himself; it may not have occurred to his advisers; nevertheless what the government is actually doing is placing these nonprofit organizations on the same basis as profit-making corporations, and as the years go by I can see the arguments of my hon. friends and those across the country who argue that there is no difference between a cooperative and a corporation reinforced by this provision, reinforced because the government is injecting into the cooperative movement something which is really foreign to that movement.
If I were asking specifically for a single provision to be removed from the proposals which the government has made, this is the one that I would choose first, because I think it strikes at the very root and basis of true cooperative movements. I am, therefore, again urging the minister to consider the removal of this particular provision in the budget resolutions. I know that the view I am expressing here this afternoon is the view which is widely held by the cooperative movement. I do not think hon. members have altogether come to a realization of what the cooperative movement really is. If I wanted to place before the committee completely the difference between a private profit-making corporation and a cooperative society, I do not think I could do better than quote the letter which was quoted by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond and the hon. menfber for Cumberland the other evening, written by the Reverend Doctor Coady of St. Francis Xavier university. That letter placed before the house clearly the fundamental difference between the two. Here is the way in which he actually put it:
Private profit business and cooperatives are specifically different kinds of business. It is logical to suspect, therefore, that no tax legislation that applies to the former would be applicable to the latter. Violence will have to be done to fundamental principles if this is tried.
That is the point I am trying to make, that you cannot inject into the cooperative movement a provision of this sort, which is foreign to the cooperative movement, without dealing a serious blow at the movement. I do not believe the government desires to deliver a serious blow against it. But I believe that the government has failed to understand the difference between what Doctor Coady speaks of as private business and what he speaks of as the cooperative movement. You cannot inject into one something that is foreign to it and expect the business to prosper.
I have kept out of the debate pretty well because I felt that the ground had been well

covered; but I am urging the minister, since I heard him speak earlier this afternoon, to reconsider the position. This is not much of a revenue producer. I do not think it will materially affect the revenue of the government; but it is a material consideration from the point of view of a cooperative society, and it injects into the cooperative something which is entirely foreign to it. In the days to come, when perhaps this parliament has gone and our successors are in our places, just as to-day we are the successors of those who in 1930 introduced amendments to the act, which we are now dispensing with, just in the same manner, I say, some sixteen years later parliament may come back and say there is no difference between a cooperative and a corporation. They both pay interest on the capital employed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They do not have to pay it. They pay the tax if they do not pay it.
They must compute taxable interest before they pay patronage dividends, or before they can expand their business.

speechtext: As usual, my hon. friend has stated his.point with clarity and conciseness. You are not asking us to agree with all that the McDougall commission says?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, but my hon. friend is asking the government to give consideration to the special character of cooperative enterprise, and all the points he has been making were made fully before the McDougall commission. That is the whole point. I agree with my hon. friend; I do not think the tax revenue from

Income War Tax
this provision will be large because I think it will affect most cooperatives little, if at all. But I say that it maintains a principle which, in my judgment, it is most important to maintain, namely, that when a person in this country, whether it is a cooperative association, a corporation or an individual taxpayer, earns something which is taxable income, then it should be taken into account and a tax paid on it.
