The difference between the minister and myself is that he is regarding the cooperative as a corporation;-
Mr. ABBOTT; Or an association or an individual.
I am not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The individual would be in the same position.
I am not; I am regarding a cooperative as a group of individuals who are doing business with themselves individually.

I rise to support the position taken by the cooperative union of Canada and the various cooperatives that have wired and written me, and the arguments put forward in this debate to which I have listened with a great deal of interest. I refer particularly to the arguments adduced by hon. members to my right. I am not going to repeat these arguments; I support them.
I just wish to make a few observations in connection with this matter and perhaps to bring out one or two points which have been overlooked to date. The government appointed a royal commission to investigate the taxation of cooperatives. That is to the credit of the government. The appointment of the commission has had quite an effect in Canada. I am sure that many hon. members noticed that, when the commission held its sittings new public interest in cooperatives was aroused. I noticed that particularly in British Columbia. The sittings were often attended by quite a large number of people and in addition to that, the press carried extensive reports of the proceedings. That has had a tremendous effect on Canadian opinion and the Canadian people's understanding of the cooperative movement. That is one of the reasons why to-day the government, in its defence of its stand in this matter of the taxation of cooperatives, has to give further consideration to the pressure being put on by the cooperative movement, and to public opinion. We find the fishermen of the mari-times, the French-Canadian farmers, the Ontario farmers, the prairie farmers, the fisher-63260-257
men of the Pacific coast, the fruit-growers of British Columbia and the dairy cooperatives throughout all the provinces have united in their stand against the government's present tax proposals. I submit that in this issue we have had a demonstration of national unity around a principle which goes beyond race, creed or occupation.
As I said before, the government has reacted to the pressure of the cooperative movement. It has bowed to public opinion and has made certain amendments to the tax proposals. Personally I wish the government would go farther, as the previous speaker said, and delete this three per cent proposal. But I understand the government's position. At the last election they received a mandate from the people to operate the free enterprise system. At the same time they plastered the country with slogans about building a new social order. Therefore they are somewhat between the devil and the deep sea in this matter. It reminds me of what a friend said to me on one occasion. Ho said:	"I always
look on the Conservative party as a porcupine. It is exclusive, and its bristles are rather inclined to rise if you trespass on its preserves. I look upon the Liberal party as a rabbit." I asked why. He said: "It is always timid when it is facing a new set of conditions." That is what I think this government is at the present time. It does not realize the conditions which it is facing. I might say further that I asked the same party what he thought of the C.C.F.; what animal would he describe them by? He said: "Oh, a beaver, always building."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He must have been a member of the C.C.F.

Aside from that, does the government realize that the cooperative movement has revitalized the fishing industry on the Pacific coast, has done an immense amount of good for the farmers of Quebec, has been the cause of building up a dairying industry in this country, has saved the wheat situation on the prairies, has made it possible for the fishermen on the Pacific coast to earn a decent living, has salvaged the fruit growing industry in British Columbia? In doing that, the cooperative movements have actually saved the taxpayers of this country far more money than would be lost if this taxation proposal were removed. I suggest to the Acting Minister of Finance to give this question consideration from the point of view of the value of the cooperatives to the Canadian economy as a whole, on the basis of principle, and the value of the cooperatives in saving the government money.

I made my contribution to this debate this morning; but there is one point that I wish to make now, namely, that the Acting Minister of Finance constantly comes back to the fact that the McDougall report was unanimous. The Minister of Finance took the position that this is what the cooperative people and the people of Canada want and therefore the government is giving it to them. I agree that the report was unanimous, but that unanimity was bought at the expense of certain definite reservations. I know that Mr. Arnason, who was a member of that commission, certainly does not believe that cooperatives make a profit. While the McDougall report so states categorically, I want it on the record that that report was just a compromise. The cooperatives' side of the argument was also cop-promised before the decision was made unanimous. I think that is a clear statement of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Mr. Arnason made no reservations on the point to which my hon. friend is now referring.

May I also make a little contribution to this debate. My contribution may not be large; nevertheless I consider that it may be valuable; at least I think it is going to be. I rise because I feel in duty bound to say something on the basis that I, too, have received a good deal of correspondence, form letters, cards, briefs, telegrams and private interviews in respect of the whole matter of the taxation of cooperatives. If I were to review the position in which I find myself I would have to say, first, that the royal commission made their report almost a year ago. I believe it was on September 25, 1945, if my memory serves me correctly. Almost immediately there began to flow into my office a number of requests. I found that most of these were printed form cards. I suppose all hon. members received their fair share of these cards. Generally speaking, the cards requested that I should take a stand that private enterprise and cooperatives be taxed on the same basis. I thought those cards should have an answer, and I was not alone in sending out a personal letter to each of those who had sent in these printed cards. I might say, in passing, that I received about 350 of them-more than some members, and not as many as others. I felt there might be such a thing as those who had signed the cards not being completely informed in respect of all that might be involved in the subject.
However, I wrote each of them a personal letter, pointing out one or two recommendations made in the report of the royal com-

mission on cooperatives, and asking for any comments they cared to make in the matter. I believe I am not doing any harm by disclosing the fact that in answer to those 350 letters I received only eight replies. The eight I received showed considerable intelligence, and a number of them were several pages in length. These letters indicated to me that the few who replied had an extensive knowledge of their subject. It is needless to say, however, that only eight replies to 350 letters was disappointing. This all happened after the report of the royal commission had been submitted, but before the budget was brought down.
After the budget was presented, the picture changed to some extent. Then my office began to be flooded with a different type of request. Telegrams and letters began to come in, and further briefs were submitted, all asking me to take a somewhat different stand. It was suggested that, generally speaking, I should remain pretty well within the confines of the recommendations made by the royal commission.
Might I revert to a discussion of those few letters I received in answer to the form card? They were sent to me by small merchants, small businessmen who were operating what would be described as private enterprises. I fancy that many small businessmen would have said many of the things which were said in those eight replies. It was pointed out to me in those replies that the waiters were small businessmen such as clothiers, grocers, operators of general stores, and garage operators. They complained that they were being taxed on their meagre profits.
It is all very well to say that private enterprise builds up huge profits, but it must be remembered that that does not apply to all people who are in business under the private enterprise system. Nearly all my constituency is composed of either rural municipalities or small towns, and I found that many of the small businessmen in those areas find it difficult to keep their heads above water. Indeed, had it not been for the war, and a general expansion of credit with more money in circulation, many of them would have gone broke long ago.
Some of these people take this attitude: Why should my small profits be taxed when other individuals who are more wealthy than I am but who are members of a cooperative movement can take advantage of certain advantages which apply to cooperatives but do not apply to me? That is another side of the picture. I do not want it to be interpreted that I am against cooperatives. I

Income War Tax
cannot possibly be against them, because I cannot bring my mind to the point of thinking that people should not be permitted to get together to cooperate with each other in carrying on business for themselves. The principle of it seems right, to me. For that reason I favour cooperatives, and I want to do all I can to foster the spirit which actuates their formation.
At the same time, there is the other picture in respect of small private businesses struggling in outlying districts. I put in a word for them. Generally speaking, I must support the position taken by the royal commissioners, for I find that most of the briefs sent to me favour that report. There may be some details wherein there are differences of opinion, but these are on matters of administration.
In trying to think my way through the maze of complications surrounding this matter of the taxation of cooperatives, compared with the taxation of private business, I cannot help asking myself why we are really fighting about this matter. I wonder if we have really got down to asking ourselves that question, and trying to answer it. Is there any need to fight about it? I suppose, if we want to attempt to run the country under a restricted system, then perhaps we shall have to fight.
But why do we fight? What is wrong? There must be something wrong or we would not have to fight. Are we short of anything? I know we are not living in normal times to-day; but legislation of this type is not imposed upon the people for a specific year or because of the exigencies of the times. Legislation of this type is put upon the books and will remain there forever or until it is lifted again. It is put on the books because the present administration is operating under a certain financial arrangement. They refuse to move away from the rules and regulations imposed upon society by that system. In normal times wre are not short of anything; the only thing we seem to be short of is money. That is why we are fighting over the shortage. We have an industrial relations committee sitting at the present time. What are they fighting over?

I want to pursue my illustration, Mr. Chairman, but I am afraid you will call me to order again if I do, and perhaps I should not impose upon your generosity, your fairness and your kindness. I want a satisfactory answer to that. I am not saying that under the present system we can do away with all taxation, but it seems to me that we are going too far. The hon. member for Cariboo passed out a few bouquets to the Minister of Finance. He said he was a most capable individual and had done a marvellous job. All my Liberal friends over there began to pound their desks. Then he went on to say that the Acting Minister of Finance was coming right along in his tracks, and the Liberals patted their desks again. Well, I did not pat my desk. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a strong statement.

That is a strong statement. If the government takes anything from my pocket it is taking something that belongs to me. A union man once spoke to me in terms of "take-home pay", and I said, "What do you mean by 'take-home pay'? Don't you take it all home?" I feel, within myself-I am not referring to the acting minister or the Minister of Finance-that this legislation is being introduced on the advice of big business to curb the activities and the expansion of the cooperative movement, which has done so much for the rank and file of this country.

There has been a lot of discussion, and if most of the members who have spoken on cooperatives would spend their time in advising the government how to cut taxation they would not have to worry about the tax on cooperatives. Under the

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, and with the unanimous consent of the house, I should like to make a brief statement.
In order to clear up a misconception which may have been created by some press and radio announcements yesterday, I think it may be well for rjie to explain to the house the present position as regards UNRRA purchases of canned fish from Canada's 1946 production. Briefly, these announcements, which apparently originated in Halifax, were to the effect that UNRRA had asked Canada to release it from its commitment to purchase 30.000.000 pounds of canned herring, mackerel and chicken haddie and that thereby the maritime canners had been placed in a serious position.
What has actually happened is that UNRRA has asked to be relieved of this commitment as far as possible; but, at the same time, it has expressed its readiness to purchase whatever part of the 30,000,000 pounds, whether a large part or small, that Canada is unable to market through other channels. In other words, the commitment holds, even up to the total amount of 30,000,000 pounds if necessary.

Government departments, my own and the Department of Trade and Commerce, are exploring the possibility of finding other export outlets for some of this canned fish. On the domestic side, the wartime prices and trade board has recently lifted all restrictions as to the quantities of these products which may be released in Canada. In this way it may be possible to relieve UNRRA of some part of its commitment by disposing of some of the fish through other channels, but UNRRA will remain committed to take from us the remaining part of the 1946 output making up the 30,000,000 pounds. Thus the herring, chicken haddie and1 mackerel canners are assured of market outlet for this full quantity.

I should like to make use of this first opportunity I have had to discuss the resolution since the minister gave notice of the fact that two important changes have been made in what originally had been planned for the taxation of cooperatives. I wish to compliment the minister and the government, and to thank them on behalf of the cooperatives for the faltering step they did take. Even if it was done hesitatingly, at the same time it gives some of us the satisfaction of knowing that when occasionally we raise our voices the government listens. That is good, so far as it goes. The agreement to extend the period from six months to twelve months for the payment of patronage dividends is at least of some benefit to the cooperatives. The same observation would apply to the government's willingness not to compel cooperatives to treat members and non-members alike in connection with the payment of patronage dividends, a provision which is of considerable importance to the cooperative movement. As has been pointed out previously in the house, with benefits and privileges go some distinct responsibilities and obligations. Therefore I am pleased to see that the government has gone to this extent.
That leaves us with a resolution which still contains two undesirable features, from the point of view of the cooperative movement. The Minister of Finance on a number of occasions has objected to a reference to what has been called the retroactive feature in the taxation; nevertheless that is what people out in the country consider it to be, and it is something of great concern to some cooperative organizations.
As previously pointed out, this government and those which have preceded it are to blame for the situation in which the cooperatives find themselves to-day. Had we had a piuper dominion cooperatives act which would have given cooperative organizations fromi one end of the country to the other a proper yardstick with which to govern themselves, in all probability we would not find ourselves in this position to-day. Furthermore, as has been pointed out, a former minister of finance in moving an amendment to this act some years ago-and this has been placed on record'-distinctly told the house at that time that it was the intention of the government to make provision for cooperatives.
The question was asked this afternoon respecting the exact amount involved, and how much the taxation would bring to the treasury. While I admit that is important, yet to my mind there is something more fundamental in this than the mere counting of dollars and
cents. Consequently I say that the principle involved is of more concern to the people of this country and to the cooperatives in particular than are the actual dollars and cents, even though they may amount to quite a sum.
There is a second feature that I take serious objection to being retained in this resolution. I refer to the three per cent clause. I wish the Minister of Finance, the Acting Minister of Finance and their colleagues in the government would realize that the principal motive of the people who comprise the cooperative movement, their thought and their desire when they banded together, was not the return that they might get on the money invested but the service that they could render to the community.
The story has been told many times in this house, and I have no doubt that there are many members in the present parliament who have a working knowledge of how these different cooperative organizations were formed. However, I fail to see where that knowledge and understanding has been of any benefit to the government in bringing down this legislation. It is not my intention to take up the time of the committee or to weary hon. members, but I should like to give a brief resume of the history of cooperative organizations. In order to shorten that resume, I shall deal with only one organization which has been mentioned a number of times this afternoon, the wheat pools of western Canada. I want to assure hon. members from other parts of Canada that when we speak of the wheat pools we are speaking of only one part of the cooperatives, and we know that other parts are vitally interested.
I well recall in years gone by when we did not have a cooperative organization in so far as the marketing of grain in western Canada was concerned. A former minister of agriculture who sat on the same side on which members of the government now sit, the late Doctor Motherwell, played a most important part along with other people in forming the original grain growers' association of western Canada in an attempt to obtain some redress from the treatment that the farmers were receiving from the grain trade of that day.
We had a suspicion, in fact we had fairly definite knowledge that the grain trade of that day were not giving the farmers a square deal. It was commonly said that an elevator agent who could not make enough in operating an elevator for one year to paj' for the elevator three times over was of no use to the elevator company. I have seen a farmer drive-in forty or fifty miles with a little jag of grain. When he got to town the agent would examine the
Income War Tax

wheat and say, "That is a nice sample of No. 1, but I am sorry, I have room only for No. 3". The farmer had to take No. 3 price or haul his load home for another forty or fifty miles.
We had knowledge of those things. From the old united grain growers' association we established the Saskatchewan cooperative elevator company. In establishing that company we had a desire, not to make a profit on the money we invested, but to build a cooperative that would give us service and a fair share of the consumer's dollar. However, in building up that organization we did not accomplish what we had hoped to accomplish. I would not say that we were deliberately misled; but it finally turned out that, while there was a decided improvement in the service, while an attempt was made to give service in preference to making a return on investment, we still did not attain that cooperative principle for which we were striving. In the final analysis, the cooperative elevator company was run on the basis of a return for the money invested. As an example, if I hauled all my grain to the cooperative elevator I would not receive any more in proportion to the money I had invested than would the man who did not haul a single bushel.
As things went on, we could see more and more that we had not built our structure properly. In spite of the fact that the elevator company was giving improved service at reduced cost, we were piling money on top of money. Shares which cost S7.50 went up to 850, after the original investment had been returned time after time in the form of dividends. That confirmed the idea that we had that we were not getting a fair share of the consumer's dollar for the grain that we had been putting into the different elevators of this country.
That is what brought on the next step, the formation of the wheat pools and the subsidiary pool elevators. We learned from the mistakes of the past that if we were to build a true cooperative we had to get away from the idea of obtaining a return on our money. What we tried to do was to build an organization that would give the individual farmer a fair return on the consumer's dollar that was paid for his grain. I do not need to go over the history of the wheat pools. They had their ups and they had their downs, but throughout the years they have endeavoured to adhere to the principle that, instead of getting a return of money on the investment, the main concern should be to give service to the members and endeavour to obtain for them a fair share of the consumer's dollar.

As has been pointed out, for a considerable number of years the Department of National Revenue did not assess the wheat pools. Finally they came to the conclusion, rightly or wrongly I would not say, that under the act as it was and in spite of what the Minister of Finance has said in years gone by, the pools should be assessed. They intimated to the pools at that time that if they were not satisfied they could take the case to the courts and it would not cost them any more than if the government took the case to the courts itself. But no sooner had that action been taken than the government blocked it all by appointing the royal commission. That stopped any further litigation.

In Saskatchewan we formed the consumers' cooperative refinery, which brought about equally beneficial results for the consumer of gasoline in Saskatchewan, not in the way of returns on the money invested, but in giving service to the people of the province. It seems, however, that the government is determined to make those of us who do not believe that the wages of money must be given first consideration accept that principle. Those of us who have banded ourselves together in cooperative movements have done

We say that on any money that we as individual members of a cooperative receive in the way of patronage dividends and returns from our respective organizations we are prepared to pay income tax just like any other citizen, but we contend that the money that we put into the cooperative is the money of the individual and not the corporation's money to be used with the idea of making profits to pay dividends to certain shareholders. If a person does not want to do business with our cooperative, regardless of what that cooperative organization may be, that is his right and privilege and he can go ahead and do business with any other organization or company. But we contend that we have built up an organization that has striven for the advancement of the community instead of piling up profits on top of profits, and that we should not be penalized for doing that. I repeat I am satisfied that the government is determined to force upon the cooperatives of this country the idea that the wages of money come before service to the community.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, have I the right to speak? A moment ago we had a vote on the amendment proposed by the government to its own resolution. To that amendment I saw nobody in this chamber vote in opposition. We now have before us the government's resolution as amended. That resolution as amended by the government this party will not support, and for this reason. The government, after many months-in fact after some years of study-after it has had a commission examine into this whole question, brings in a proposal with respect to the taxation of cooperatives. On two or three features of that policy it has changed its mind since its proposal was introduced, changed its mind on the suggestion and with the approval of nearly the whole house. But two taxes still remain in the government's programme: one, a tax on three per cent of the employed capital of cooperatives-a tax to be applied in future. That is one considered policy of the government with respect to the taxation of cooperatives in this country.
But with respect to the past, during which time the government imposed no tax on cooperatives, and during much of the time did not try to collect any, the law officers of the crown, whom it assigned to interpret legislation which was not intended to tax cooperatives, have recently interpreted the legislation to mean that it can tax cooperatives. In the light of that circumstance, certain of these large cooperatives did not pay patronage dividends over the last two years; they held the money back which would otherwise have been paid out-held it back in order to have funds to meet the threat of possible taxation. It is held there in huge sums; and on the basis of the tax laws of the past this government is saying in effect, "Now we are going to tax three of the large cooperatives in western Canada to the extent of millions of dollars. For the future these organizations will pay less than $300,000 a year; but for the last two years we are going to make them pay possibly ten or fifteen times that amount each
Income War Tax

year." They are now discussing just how much the latter tax will be

a proposed compromise on the legislation as it was.
My position is this. If it is wise policy from now on to tax these cooperative organizations, in round figures-because that is all we can get-say less than 8300.000 a year, this government cannot justify taxing these organizations ten or fifteen times that much for the last two years. For that reason we shall have to oppose this resolution as amended.

The amendment
improved the resolution; but, as the leader of the opposition has stated, the amended resolution is, except for that slight amendment, as objectionable as ever. The principle is wrong. What the leader of the opposition has said in regard to the taxation of the large cooperatives is, I think, justified. This afternoon I objected strenuously to the three per cent feature of the resolution, and because of the unsatisfactorily amended resolution we shall oppose the resolution as amended.

I have been deliberately refraining from much talk on this whole resolution because I wanted to learn exactly what it was that the government intended to do. There have been so many confusions in the course of the debate thus far that it has been most difficult to get at the kernel of the truth; but I think I now see the whole situation quite clearly, and I am definitely and unalterably opposed to the idea of applying that three per cent tax. My objection is not based on what will happen or what has happened or what could happen, we will say, retroactively with respect to the wheat pools-important as that matter is-so much as it is upon this principle of placing the cooperatives in exactly the same category as other corporations. If there are true cooperatives in this country-and there must be a good many true cooperatives-they certainly cannot be placed in the same category for taxation purposes as an ordinary corporation. The principle involved is to my mind, an important one, and the resolution as amended certainly does not in any way appeal to me.
I shall oppose it with all my strength.

I happened to be out of the chamber, attending various committees, during this discussion, and I have not had an opportunity of making any statement regarding this matter. I have no desire to speak at length, but I believe that the whole situation with respect to what is proposed ought to be clarified. I cannot find out what is proposed under the resolution and the amendments of

the resolution. The meaning, significance and impact of this three per cent proposal are indistinctly understood.
I have a feeling, and have had ever since the campaign was developed against cooperatives, that there is in this country a body of men that is deliberately aiming to destroy cooperatives; and I do not believe that the present proposals of the government are entirely without a devious hidden influence somewhere seeking to accomplish that nefarious objective. The campaign which was conducted throughout western Canada in an endeavour to bewilder and confuse the people with respect to cooperatives and their taxation was financed with tremendous sums of money. That money did not come from any group of people who wrere anxious about the dominion government getting that much more revenue; it came from a group of people desirous of destroying cooperatives, and the only reason they wished to destroy cooperatives was that they had found that the cooperatives were doing the work for which they were organized, namely protecting the individual citizen throughout Canada against, the rapacious greed of monstrous organizations aiming at the destruction of the common man.
That is precisely the situation; and in order to clarify matters so that the committee may know where it is going and what it is doing, I would make this proposal. Let the government withdraw the proposal to tax cooperatives at the present time and devote at least a year to the clarification of the situation. Nowhere have I been able to find, even in the commission's report, a distinct and clearly demarcated definition of what constitutes a cooperative and what does not. Neither do I find in the speeches of hon. members on the government side or in the legislation which is apparently proposed any exact definition of what constitutes a cooperative. Merely to pass a law to tax cooperatives, when we have no idea what we are going to tax is, I consider, a reckless procedure.
It may be argued that if we pass the law and find later on that it is undesirable we can rescind it. That is simply not the way matters work in democracies. No matter how pernicious a law is, it will be next to impossible for us to organize a body of public opinion sufficiently strong to repeal it once it is passed.
I should like to make some suggestions; but, before doing so, I would read a statement made last January by Clinton B. Anderson, United States secretary of agriculture. I am quoting an excerpt from his speech, taken

Income War Tax
from the Alberta wheat pool budget of July 19, from an article entitled, "Clamps Down on Cooperatives":
When I think of farm cooperatives I think of them not as complex business concerns, but as groups of independent farmers banded together to do some job that is too big for them as individuals. They are not seeking profits as a group, hut are seeking to use modern business methods to maintain their way of life. It is this basic objective of farm cooperatives that has caused congress and the courts to recognize generally and in specific legislation the right of tarmers to organize cooperatives and the public welfare obligation of cooperatives. Shorn of all technicalities, it is this basic purpose that frees cooperatives from income tax.
I believe that with the sentiments of that statement virtually every member of this house is in accord, whether he be on the Liberal side or on the opposition side. I wager that eighty per cent of the members of the house are in sympathy with these remarks; yet at the present time we have no assurance whatsoever that the legislation proposed by the government is in accord with the spirit of these words. We have no such evidence at all. We need to know exactly what is a genuine cooperative. The definition ought to be worked out with minutest care by men thoroughly qualified for the task.
Of all the organizations in Canada at present operating under the name of cooperatives, exactly which ones can qualify under the definition implied in Mr. Clinton Anderson's statement, and precisely why? That question every hon. member ought to be able to answer, but there is hardly one of us who is capable of giving an answer to it, simply because we have not the information at our disposal. On the other hand, which organizations cannot so qualify, and precisely why? That is something which we ought to know.
All this ought to be worked out, first of all; the facts should be publicized in every nook and corner of the dominion, and every cooperative should be given at least a year in which to bring its organization and practices into conformity with principles universally accepted as those of genuine, bona fide cooperatives. Until this is done, we are in no position, either as a house or as a country, to pronounce on the important matter of the taxation of cooperatives. I submit in all earnestness that the government should withdraw these resolutions and allow the people of Canada to know exactly what is being proposed with respect to their welfare where the taxation of cooperatives is undertaken.

Most of the cooperatives which have been formed took over existing businesses. That was the only way they could get a quota of stock to sell. In most rural areas and small towns we find that it is much better for all concerned for the cooperative being formed to take over an existing business rather than set up a competitive business and perhaps put out of business someone else who is serving the community. Am I to understand that if a cooperative is formed in that way it will not be allowed to obtain exemptions for the three years as will other cooperatives which are formed and do not take over an existing business?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As indicated in the minister's speech, that was the intention, although it is not so specified in this resolution. The real purpose of the exemption to a new cooperative is to enable it to get on its feet. If a cooperative takes over an existing business which is already established and has a clientele, has inventory, has working capital and all that kind of thing, it does not need-
It will not have working capital.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It may or it may not; it will depend on the type of cooperative. If it takes over an established business it has not the same need for this exemption, for what it may be worth. It certainly should not be the intention of this or any other legislation to encourage groups of individuals to take over existing businesses and be prepared to convert them into cooperative enterprises, which, in some cases, might be for the purpose of obtaining tax exemptions.

May I just say a word on this resolution? I know some members of the committee feel that the cooperatives are inclined to deal rather harshly economically with existing small businesses. I know there is nothing that any cooperative has done-if what is alleged is correct-which may equal what is proposed under this legislation. This is what is happening in many of the smaller towns in western Canada. The farmers organize a cooperative society. Instead of going into a town and competing with the merchant already established there and put-
ting him out of business because of the membership at large in the community, the cooperative goes in and suggests to the business man that they are going to organize anyway. He has an established business there and on a fair basis they are prepared to take over his business. In many instances of which I know they appoint the owner of the store the manager of the business. As a matter of fact I know that some of the managers of these stores-and I have several in mind at the moment-who have accepted such a proposition are to-day actually better off than they were as independent merchants in the villages. In the interest of equity, and from every other point of view, I say that the explanation given by the minister in the budget speech is frequently against the interests of the small businessman in the area where the cooperative starts up. What you are going to do is to say to the people in the community-and I have particularly in mind the farmers in a given community-you may start a cooperative society, but if you take over an existing business you cannot get the same relief as you would if you started a new business of your own.
With regard to what the minister says concerning a business established with its own working capital, I would ask him to think it over. I do not think it is a sound argument. As a matter of fact a cooperative organized to take over a business begins in exactly the same way as a cooperative starting a new business. It has to raise working capital in the same way; it has to do its business in the same way as any other cooperative beginning business would do. On the other hand, if the interpretation given by the minister in his budget speech to the words "commencing business" is adhered to, in many instances it will work a hardship on men who have established a small business and who might otherwise be protected by coming into the cooperative and acting as managers for the cooperative society. The minister should give consideration to that point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Let me say at once that there is nothing in the resolution which would preclude that, and on this particular point, whatever it may have been on some others, my mind is completely open. I shall be glad to give consideration to that point and to discuss it with my colleagues. In its terms the resolution does not preclude it; it is in broad general terms.

I am thinking of the budget speech.	.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I mentioned that. I pointed out, as the minister indicated in his budget speech, that was the intention.
What is the position of a cooperative which was formed in 1944?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is not affected at all by this resolution.
Will it have exemption from taxes for three years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; this applies to the ones commencing after December 31, 1946.

Then the minister is making a distinction there. This resolution should be framed in such a way as to include a cooperative which started in 1945. As it reads now, it refers to cooperatives starting in 1946.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We do not like retroactive legislation.

It does not need to be retroactive. Start from this year and say that from this year it will not be taxed. It is not retroactive so long as it is made applicable to cooperatives which started in 1945 or 1944. It would simply mean that the cooperative which started in 1944 would have one year in which it would be free from taxation; the one which started in 1945 would have two years, and the one which started in 1946 would have three years. The minister will have to do that to make the legislation fair.

I was delighted to hear the minister say that he had an open mind on resolution 16, because there is one particular aspect which interests me very much. During the war years, cooperatives starting up could start only by buying out existing businesses. Under the wartime controls they were not allowed to start new businesses. I happen to know of one case because I was a shareholder and it was in my home town. The only way they could start up was by buying out a retired merchant. It meant that we had to raise a substantial amount of money to take over. We had to pay for the business in cash and we were crippled for lack of liquid capital; we were crippled in the matter of stocking our shelves with merchandise because we were forced to put out such a large outlay to begin business. Had we been able to start under other circumstances, we might have been able to rent a building and we would have had only the cost of rental, but we were forced to buy a building which contained living quarters and which was much larger than the sort of unit we would have started with ordinarily. I am sure that there are many cooperatives in this position. From the beginning they are forced to purchase existing businesses. They are forced to put out a large amount of available capital in order to get started. Anything that will make it difficult for them to carry on will be a crippling move, and I am glad to hear that the minister is open to conviction.

I was interested in the answer which the minister gave to the hon. member for Melfort in connection with the three-year exemption from taxation. Had the answer been more favourable, I would not have thought it necessary to move an amendment. However, in view of the attitude taken, I move the following amendment:
That resolution No. 16 pertaining to Income War Tax Act be amended by striking out the words "commencing business after December 31, 1916" as such words appear in lines 1 and 2 of the said resolution.
The effect of that amendment would be that any cooperative commencing operations in 1944, 1945 or 1946 would come in under the exemption, the same as the others.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As my hon. friend probably anticipates, I am obliged to take the stand that his amendment is out of order, having been moved by a private member. Clearly, if adopted, it would alter the balance of ways and means for the current year, and would render cooperatives which might otherwise be taxable exempt from taxation. Therefore I must take the stand that it is out of order.
Will the minister allow this whole resolution to stand, in view of the representations made, and give consideration to the various aspects of it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If the committee insists I will allow it to stand. I have pointed out that it is in broad terms, with the exception of the point now raised by the hon. member for Dauphin. But I also point out that section 4(p) of the Income War Tax Act will continue in force until December 31,1946. So that whatever rates are available to cooperatives under section 4(p) will continue until that date, and the new legislation will become effective as and from January 1. 1947. Therefore I think it is consistent to give a three-year period of complete exemption from January 1, 1947. I shall give further, and perhaps even sympathetic consideration to the point raised by the hon. members for Rose-town-Biggar, Melfort and Qu'Appelle, as to the question of extending the privilege to a cooperative which acquired an existing business.
However, I must take the stand that any amendment to change the date is out of order and, in fairness, I should add that I would have to have much more convincing
Income War Tax

reasons than have thus far been offered to make me change my view that we should make the commencement of this exemption period coincide with the effective repeal of section 4(p).
I should hope that, subject to further discussion on the general principle, the committee could accept the resolution, thereby enabling us to proceed with the others.

I appreciate that the minister will give consideration to the points raised, but I should also like him to give consideration to the matter of cooperatives formed in 1944 or 1945. Under section 4(p) they may be, and in many cases are exempt from taxation. Now they will find that when section 4(p) is revoked they will be taxable. The fact is that they will be taxable for the last year, upon which they would not otherwise be taxable if they were new cooperatives being formed in 1947. There would be two years in the case of one, and one year in the case of the other, under section 4(p). But now they become taxable. I believe it will be found to work out in that way. An unfairness will be created there, unless this provision applies to all cooperatives as from 1947, whether thev were formed in 1945, 1946 or 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will think over the point raised by the hon. member. Frankly I do not think there is any danger of their being involved.

In view of the statement
made by the minister that he would give sympathetic consideration to the case made out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when that hon. member painted a picture of a merchant going into a village and taking over the business of another, I should like to say a word respecting a similar situation, and approaching it from a different angle.
Two merchants are competitors in the same village. They carry on in a friendly way, doing business and serving the community for years in a satisfactory manner. A cooperative comes to one store and says to the owner, "We have a proposition whereby you will turn over your business to us and we will make you our manager. If you do not do that we will open another store in competition with you. Because of our membership and the friendly feeling existing toward us in the community, you can figure out for yourself what wall happen to you."
Because of that pressure, one of the merchants gives way, sells his business and takes the position of manager. He is now in competition with the second merchant across the

street. One of these merchants enjoys a three-year exemption, while the other suffers no handicap at all.
In the course of time the cooperative organization will set up certain profits, perhaps in the form of patronage dividends. The other evening the sum of $25 was mentioned, of which $10 is kept and $15 goes back into the business. The reserve is set up until such time as they have sufficient money to spend S500 or S600 for the installation of a new front. Notwithstanding the fact that the prices in the two stores may be the same, people will naturally turn to the one with the most attractive front, and with the better window lighting. Because of the reserve and the handicaps set in his way, the second storekeeper would be placed in an unfair position. That is why I should like to see fair taxation for all types of business.

A minute ago the minister said that he had an open mind, and that he would possibly give sympathetic consideration to the suggestion made. Then he qualified his statement by saying that he had not yet heard any convincing evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That was on the other
point.

I believe it applied to both these points. If the minister will turn to his copy of the McDougall commission report he will find at page 45 the most convincing evidence in support of our contention. I would ask him to direct his attention to paragraph 7 on that page, and the seventh line in that paragraph where he will find these words:
. . . with the consent of the minister, be exempt from income tax for its first three fiscal periods following the commencement of operations.
That was the recommendation mentioned by the hon. member for Melfort. I do not offer it in any spirit of criticism, but I believe the minister will see the justice of it.
I should like to point out one important cooperative which will be affected by the proposals in resolution 16 of the budget resolutions, and the minister's statement respecting the budget, to the effect that this three-year exemption will not be applicable to those who begin operations prior to December 31, 1946. In the budget speech it is indicated that those who take over an existing business will not be exempt, either.
We have in Swift Current what is known as the cooperative horse-marketing association, through which we pack horse meat for Belgium and UNRRA. We have found through the years that the ranchers who used to be in the

Income War Tax
horse-raising business, when it was a good business, have found that the country now needs cattle more than it does horses. Horses are very hard on grazing land because they clip close to the ground like sheep.
A couple of years ago, in an attempt to get rid of these horses a marketing and packing organization was established under cooperative laws. They had1 great difficulty in getting started because the war was on and buildings and supplies were hard to get. There was considerable competition in the way of getting capital because campaigns were being carried on for the purchase of victory bonds and so on; yet they had to be financed. First, the Saskatchewan government guaranteed the organization to the extent of $50,000. Next, the Belgium buying committee helped them by way of advance orders. The Bank of Montreal made considerable advances on the understanding that when they became organized and the members' capital began to come in they would be reimbursed from that and from the earnings when they started to work.
They got going under those difficulties. If they had had to build a new building, as the budget indicates is necessary, they would never have got started. However, they took over an old power plant which belonged to the city of Swift Current. That was an existing business, and technically, according to the budget, that stipulation would apply to this particular case. On both counts this new association is going to suffer severely unless the minister gives more than sympathetic consideration to its case. That is one reason why I believe the most convincing argument I could offer is the recommendation of the McDougall commission.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This goes farther than the McDougall commission recommended. As my hon. friend has pointed out, the McDougall commission recommends that it be with the consent of the minister. In other words, they were suggesting that another of these discretions to which objection has been taken in some cases should be conferred upon the minister. The resolution proposes that the exemption will be given as of right; there will be no discretion in the minister to approve or refuse it. That is why I say the proposed legislation goes farther than the McDougall commission recommended.

That is quite correct so far as those who started after December 31, 1946. are concerned; but it is not so good, as I think the minister will admit, with regard to the case to which I referred. I believe they should receive some consideration because they have done a useful job for that part of
the country and for the world. Poland and Belgium are very happy about it, as is UNRRA.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member has almos convinced me to eat horse meat.
I would be glad to gm you a can because I have one upstairs.
Until what age does a horse remain palatable?

Mr. Chairman, is this germane to the discussion? I am not an expert on the packing of horse meat. They have an expert at the plant who decides what horses shall be used. They are graded according to the amount of flesh.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Old horses are better than young ones.

That is my opinion.
Generally speaking, horses between five and ten years of age in good flesh are considered the best. Those are range horses, and they are always good.

May I say just a word to the senior member for Halifax because probably the minister wdll read what the hon. member said and what I said in connection with the taking over of an existing business. Of course, what the senior member for Halifax said is true to a large degree. If a cooperative society with a large membership came into a community where there were two stores and made a proposition to one of the storekeepers to sell out to the society and take over the management, that new cooperative store would then be entering into competition with the other store which was not taken over and which was already in existence. I submit that the argument that the new cooperative society has an unfair advantage is not soundly based. I take it from the legislation before us that we all recognize that a cooperative society is on an entirely different footing from that of a private profit-making business.
In what way?

I quoted what Doctor Coady had to say this afternoon. I shall not repeat the quotation, but Doctor Coady made this statement:
The essence of private profit business is that the businessman takes a toll from his fellow human beings-legitimate in some eases, and positively unjust in other cases. In cooperatives on the other hand no member of the firm or company-to use the terminology of old-line business-can take a toll from his fellows. Any money he receives back in the shape of patronage dividends is his own money. These dividends are overcharges that were made by him-
Income War Tax

self in the course of a year's business. By no stretch of the imagination, therefore, can patronage dividends be called profit or income.
I think that is sound. The hon. member for Swift Current made a statement during the budget debate. I am not permitted to quote that statement, but I think I can summarize it in, this way. When a man joins a cooperative society he begins to serve himself. He puts a can of peas on the shelf for which he has already paid. Then he goes to the store to get that can of peas from the shelf. All that is required is that there shall be sufficient taken from him to put a new can of peas on the shelf. However, the cooperative society usually takes from him at the moment more for the can of peas than the actual service and the can of peas require to be taken, and at a subsequent period he gets back the overcharge. But that is not profit. Consequently the two types of business are not analogous, and that is the point we have been trying to get before the committee ever since this debate started.
Suppose I who am not a member of the cooperative society buy the can of peas?
I do not think any cooperative society objects to paying a tax on the profit made on business done with nonmembers. That has been said over and over again.
How can they keep track of purchases by non-members?

It so happens that most of us belong to cooperative societies. When we buy something in the cooperative store we are given a slip on which the purchase is registered. At the end of the year the cooperative society knows exactly what business it has done with its own members. In fact, your own number is placed on the slip for the records of the cooperative society.
If I walk into a cooperative store as a stranger and make a purchase, is the clerk going to ask me if I am a member?
He would say, "Are you a member and what is your account number?" You would then give your name and number if the clerk did not know you, but in most instances they know their own members.

I would point- out to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that there is a difference in the manner of doing business described by him and the ordinary business carried on by a cooperative store and the average so-called free enterprise store. The two stores I cited both purchase from wholesale houses;-these stores may be general or

grocery stores;-they each have a manager and two clerks and they pay the same scale of wages. The overhead in each store is about the same. It is fair to say that their overhead expenses will be on the same plane at the end of the year. They purchase $80,000 worth of goods in the course of their operations and mark them up 25 per cent, which gives them a gross profit of $20,000. Both stores sell their goods at the same price. Take a look at their windows. Peas, beans, and so on, are all ticketed at the ceiling prices, and their profit is exactly the same.
No profits in the cooperatives.
I am dealing with actual facts, not imaginary. They are definitely profits, or there is gain, the difference between the cost and the selling price.
You mean margin.

Term it anything you wish to satisfy your own mind. The fact remains that the cost is the same and the selling price is the same. You can call it profit or margin or gain; it all amounts to the same thing when you put it in the cash register and total up your profits or gains at the end of the year. As I say, there is $20,000 profit, less the operating expenses. So that the net profit or gain or margin is the same in the case of both; the consumers are all paying the same price.
You may ask, where is the difference? The difference is that the private enterprise store, No. 2 store, is paying income tax year in and year out to the government to help carry on the business of the country. The cooperative pays no tax; it pays out its profits in the way of patronage dividends, and if the member of the cooperative does not wish to hold on to them he is allowed to give back $15, we will say, out of $25 to build up a reserve. If there is any fairness in taxing one store and not the other, I may be stupid but I cannot see it.
The individual store owner puts his margin, if you wish to call is that-
I call it profit.

He puts his margin or profit into his own pocket. The cooperative society, on the other hand, does not distribute a profit but returns to the individual members the overcharge which in the other case went as profits to the individual store owner. In the case of the cooperative it is returned to the members of the organization, being an overcharge that was made in the beginning. The reason why the cooperative store has

Income War Tax
about the same mark-up as the private enterprise store is because it does not wish to enter into a price-cutting competition with the private enterprise store. As to the payment of income tax, the individual members of the cooperative society, if their incomes are large enough, pay income tax on them.
May I deal with that? There is a definite difference between the income of an individual and the income derived from the operation of a store.
What tax would store No. 2 pay, the one that was not run by the cooperative?

I wish to deal with the overcharge which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned. There is no such thing as an overcharge. When two stores set up to do business they both sell at the ceiling prices laid down by the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board. There is no overcharge. If a store tried to overcharge it could not possibly compete with the store that did not. The reason the small merchant is able to compete with the largest chain store or departmental store, no matter how big, is that he sells service to his customers. That is why the great majority of them succeed.
I am not opposed to cooperatives. I rather welcome competition on fair lines, but I certainly do not think the government or anyone else should subsidize one competitor against another. That is the whole point. You could not possibly succeed in business if you were continually overcharging your customers. Common sense will tell you that. If you adopted that course you would not last very long in business. Only by fair dealing can you carry on and build up a bigger business.
One hon. member asked me, would they not pay the same income tax? During the war, when we were paying excess profits tax over a certain standard basis, our entire profit beyond that point went to the government. But if we are allowed to distribute that excess to one hundred or one thousand individuals they in cum will pay a very much smaller amount individually, and the aggregate amount of income tax paid by these individuals on that distribution will not begin to represent the amount paid in taxation under the Excess Profits Tax Act or even under the standard profits tax by the store.
The hon. member in distinguishing between two types of business called one a free enterprise business and the other a cooperative.
Just to distinguish them.
I should like to know in what respect a cooperative business is not a free enterprise business.

I do not think it is necessary to go into detail on that. The hon. member knows my views in regard to free enterprise and individual incentive to make thp best of one's opportunities, and I know his ideas in regard to cooperatives and public ownership. But I would say this, that there is a difference between the two, and the difference is that one continues to pay income tax from January 1, 1947, right through for three years, while the other pays no tax whatsoever. Surely that is a difference.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
I hesitate to receive questions from the hon. member because I may not be able to answer them.

I am sure you can, because I make my questions extremely simple when I am addressing them to you. My thought is this. We will assume that nineteen of my hon. friends to my immediate left form a cooperative.
We are twenty-eight.

I said nineteen, because in Alberta you cannot have a partnership of over twenty people. We will also assume that nineteen of you on the other side of the house-I will leave my own party out of the discussion-also form a partnership. My hon. friends to my left open a grocery store on one side of the street in the town of X. You have a grocery store on the other side of the town of X. Your windows are dressed the same; you are selling groceries. I drive along the centre of the street in my borrowed motorcar-because I have not one at the moment-I am going out to shoot some ducks, or something of the kind, and I want some grub. I look at the windows and I go to one store or the other. Now, the cooperative pays no income tax, but the partnership does. Both adopt exactly the same methods of display and salesmanship. Will the senior member for Halifax, knowing that they adopt exactly the same methods, tell me why one should be favoured in the matter of taxation as against the other?
The hon. member always makes his questions so interesting and states them so simply, and then he surrounds them with a lot of frills. But after all-

The answer is, there should be no difference-if that will help you.

The answer I would give him is exactly the same answer as he would give me. The hon. member gave the answer to the question the other day when he asked much the same question, and cited the two stores; I agree with him and I know he agrees with me.

I think this is a time when we should take a practical view and not be merely idealistic. I can, claim a close association with the cooperative movement in Canada from its earliest beginnings in the province of Ontario and in parts of the province of Saskatchewan. But I also have the benefit of a background of municipal experience, and I know this, that one of the bugbears that municipal governments face is tax exemptions on land and on some enterprises which may be located within the municipality. I tell the committee this, that the costs of government in this country are now reaching proportions when somebody must dig down deep to raise the wherewithal to carry on.
As I view the cooperatives, the one method that they can employ to save money for their patrons is their method of purchasing. They purchase in large volume. Their costs of distribution are very little less than those of private enterprise, if there is any difference at all. The fact of the matter is that in a majority of cases the private enterprise man is probably providing his clients with some accommodation by way of credit, whereas the cooperatives will certainly seek to collect on the goods as they are sold; and quite properly so. I know that when I was associated with the Saskatchewan grain growers, whether the organization -was selling binder twine or whatever it might be. we had cash on the barrel head when we sold, while probably the fellow down the street gave a range of credit for the goods he w'as selling.
Since someone has to make -up the volume of money required, bear in mind that every time you grant an exemption somebody else must dig a little deeper. Not long ago I rose in this chamber and said that I had no objection to crown companies, provided that they bore their share of the nation's taxation; and in my contribution to this amendment, I am only trying to be consistent. I can remember that we had a motto in the Sunday school, in the days when I was interested in that particular work:
If everyone in the Sunday school is just like me, What kind of Sunday school will the Sunday school be?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is an interesting
question.

If people find a means whereby, when they call themselves cooperatives, they will be granted a preference, the net result may be that you will have many cooperatives but someone will pay the costs. So what I am suggesting is that, since the costs of government are so great, I believe every individual and every corporation and enterprise should bear its fair share of the nation's costs.

If I may be permitted to refer to the question asked by the hon. member for Calgary West, I think an answer should be given to his question, because I believe he was seeking an answer in all sincerity. May I point out there are two differences between a cooperative enterprise and the type of partnership which he described to us. In the first place, if any surplus is acquired, whether we call it profit or anything else, in the case of a cooperative it is divided on the basis of business done, while in the matter of a private business it is divided on the basis of the amount of money invested. That is one difference.
And the amount of risk taken.

That does not enter into it. The other difference, which I think is probably more important, is that in a private business, as I understand it, those who own shares have one vote for each share, or the basis is such that the more shares you own, the more control you have over the business; in fact, if you own more than half the shares you have the controlling interest in the business. In a cooperative you can own as many shares as you like, but it is "one member, one vote." No matter how much any one member invests, he has only one vote, and it continues to be a democratically run and operated enterprise. Those are the two differences.
Before I take my seat, perhaps I had better do two things at once. I am given to understand, Mr. Chairman, although you have not yet so ruled, that the amendment I have moved is out of order. I am also given to understand that if I withdraw it at this time there will be a more appropriate place to move it, on the third reading of the bill. So that with your permission I should like to withdraw my amendment at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has the hon. member leave to withdraw his amendment?
Amendment (Mr. Zaplitny) withdrawn.

I made a suggestion a moment ago which was criticized in a very kindly way-if I may use the expression of the Minister of Labour who is not

Income War Tax
here at the moment-and it was this. I suggested that nineteen people over there formed a cooperative and nineteen people there formed a partnership. Let us assume that the nineteen people in the partnership put up $100 apiece and that each had an equal vote because each had an equal investment. The answer of the hon. member was this, that in a cooperative, no matter how many shares a person owns, he only has one vote. A partnership can equally well have a partnership agreement stating the same thing. There is nothing against it in law, in equity, or in common sense. Having that in view, I hope to hear from the hon. member again, because he did say that his method was the more democratic. The most democratic thing I know of in this world is a willingness and even an eagerness to pay taxes, because that is the way the country lives. Governments have no other source of	income.	My	wholepoint is just this:	why,	because	you	use adifference in method, is there a difference in obligation? Those nineteen men, let us say, are selling to nineteen hundred people to make their profit. "Profit" is a good word and I intend to use it.	I drive along	the street;there is their store	and	there is	your	store,
and I am invited to buy at either place. In my judgment there is neither logic nor reason -perhaps they mean the same thing-why one in a matter of taxation should be treated any differently from the other.
Let us take this horrible thing, a corporation -because all you needed to do in the terrible thirties was to mention that something was a "corporation" and you could fill a hall in any part of the country and get lots of cheers if you just abused the corporation sufficiently. My hon. friend is quite right that a majority in shares, which means a majority investment, controls the corporation. In that, I frankly confess, it differs from a cooperative. If you have a real cooperative, be it a consumers' or a producers' cooperative, and a consumer, whom we will call A, buys more than B, then A will get more of the profits than B. That is the basis on which it is done. In other words, by purchase he makes a greater investment and therefore gets a greater return. What is the difference between that and a person making a greater investment in money, in buying shares, and therefore getting a greater return? speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I join with those who have tried to answer the question of the hon. member for Calgary West. I still prefer
to think of us as a group of twenty-eight, all of whom would be in the cooperative, but we will accept his example of nineteen persons forming a cooperative and nineteen others forming a partnership. We have been asked to indicate differences. One particular difference that I would point out is that the nineteen of us in the cooperative will receive back patronage dividends, or whatever you call it, from that cooperative only to the extent that we ourselves make purchases. The nineteen of us will not gain by any of the sales which we may make to the hundreds of others who come along to buy, although actually a cooperative does not work in that way; most of the others would also be members. On the other hand, the nineteen who are in the partnership share in the profit that is made from sales to the hundreds who come to buy from that store. To that should be added the fact that we nineteen who are members of a cooperative cannot and do not make our living on the basis of what we save by being members of a cooperative. We have to have some other source of income, on which we pay taxes, and it is out of that other income that we effect a saving in purchasing the things we buy from a cooperative. But the nineteen, who form a partnership and are in a position to sell goods to hundreds of customers who come in, do make their living out of the profit they make from their investment in that concern, and hence should pay taxes thereon.
One other point I would put on the record has relation to a remark made by the hon. member for Grey North. To be perfectly fair, he did not make a misstatement; but when he referred to the difficulties that municipalities have with tax exemptions, the impression may have been gained by some that maybe cooperatives were in this position. I wish to make it perfectly clear-and I think he will confirm it-that cooperatives have to and do pay taxes to the municipalities on their property.

speechtext: For obvious reasons we have to give tax relief to oil wells on a slightly different basis.
