speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A discussion of the taxation of oil wells would more properly come under resolutions 31 and 32.

May I, with the greatest deference and respect, agree with you that such discussion wmuld be more appropriate on those items. But it seems to me germane to the point as to whether or not they are to be treated in a similar manner. Certainly the drilling of an oil well is mining, in the broad sense. While the minister exempts mines for three years-and I am not complaining-I would remind him that when one opens a mine he has some idea of what is underground. The drills work this way, that way and the other way, and ore bodies are proved. But in connection with the drilling of an oil well, the drill is the only geologist found thus far which has ever been any good, because what the drill finds controls whether you lose your money or whether you get back a return. Certainly the geologist has gone a long way. We have seismographs, and all that sort of thing. The most that the sponsors for these instruments have ever claimed for them is that they can find a structure. And, that structure, having been found, no method has yet shown whether the structure will contain salt-water or oil. No scientific method has yet been found which will determine that fact. Accordingly I suggest to the minister that by the time he reaches his resolution 63260-258J
respecting oil, he should have some regard to the fact that both of these endeavours are mining endeavours, and that he might find some assistance for the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta who are so busy these days in trying to find oil.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall not answer the hon. member's point at this time, because it will be dealt with more fully on resolution 31. I would point out to him, what he probably already knows, that under section 8 (10) of the Income War Tax Act a special 50 per cent tax credit is given to oil wells for deep drilling, and the like, and that there is no comparable exemption for the mining industry.

With great respect I suggest that the acting minister is quite wrong about that. He has a special provision for deep-test wells, but no provision at all for the man who goes out in the province hon. members to my immediate left come from, and in the plains of Alberta where shallow-test drilling is found. The minister has nothing to help those people.
Let us always remember that great companies never discover oil fields. They have always been discovered by the small man who does some wild-catting, and those discoveries are later bought up by the big interests.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext:
I wish to refer to the minister's statement of last Friday evening, but I doubt whether this is the section upon which to do it. However, I have a suggestion to make to the minister on this resolution. The resolution as it is amended provides for exemption from ordinary income tax for the first three years for mining companies coming into production. My suggestion-and I believe it is an important one-is that most young mines coming into production are not profitable enough in the first three years to come under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act. Seldom do they make a profit in those years. But under the regulations of the department they are forced to make annual writeoffs for both depreciation and depletion. The write-offs are at the rate of 15 per cent per annum. So that when the three years are up and the income tax payments begin, the predevelopment charges, depreciation and depletion are written off to the extent of 45 per cent. I am speaking more to a ruling of the department than to an amendment in the section.

Income War Tax
I am asking that new mines coming into production, and exempt from taxation, shall not be forced to undertake depletion and depreciation at the rate of 15 per cent per annum for the first three years. If that is done the minister will really bring into effect the meaning and intention of section 3. If that is not done it means that the mine has virtually 50 per cent of the depreciation written off when it should be in a tax-free period.
The intent of the regulation is that mines shall be tax free for the first three years. Therefore I am asking the minister to rule thrit this shall also include suspension of depreciation and other write-offs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that that is a matter for the Minister of National Revenue in the administration of the income tax act.

I am making this plea in this house because, unless that is done, the whole intent of this resolution will be abortive. Mines do not pay taxes in the first three years because very few of them make sufficient profit, although there is occasionally one that may. If you force them to make their [DOT]write-offs at 15 per cent it means that when the three-year period is up their depreciation will be virtually 50 per cent gone, at a time when they begin their normal life of tax paying.
I realize that this is a matter for the Department of National Revenue, but I want to make the plea now, and I want to make it as strong as I possibly can, that they should not be forced to write off any part of their pre-development expenses, the cost of structures, the cost of the mill, the cost of sinking a shaft and all the other essential costs in bringing a mine into operation until such time as the first three years are up. I think that is the true intention of the framers of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As my hon. friend has pointed out, it is not a matter for legislation; it is a matter for administrative action on the part of the Minister of National Revenue.

I think this proposal is an exceedingly generous contribution to the mining industry. I should like to put this point of view before the committee. A mine or an oil well taps the natural resources of Canada and those natural resources are the property of the people of Canada. When gold or some other mineral is taken out of a mine, nothing but a hole remains and the same thing applies to oil. I know of no industry in Canada which has been as wasteful of the natural resources of the people of

Canada as the oil industry. One has only to go to the Turner valley in Alberta to see the amount of valuable gas which is being wasted, gas which could heat most of the homes in western Canada. He would then realize the valuable resources that have been wasted in that particular area.
It is always said that private enterprise is prepared to take risks, but it seems to me that much of the legislation we have adopted in this country over the last few years has been designed to take the risk away from private enterprise. To a great extent that is true of the legislation we have passed concerning the mining industry during the last number of years. Year by year we have extended to the mining industry valuable concessions in the way of being able to write off certain depreciation, to have allowances made for prospecting done, and now we come to a proposal which will give new mines complete exemption for three years. Where is the risk to capital in proportion to the rewards which they expect? If a rich mine is found the profits that accrue are out of all proportion to the amount of money invested in the undertaking.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
How many
mines do not find anything?

It is quite true that a large number do not produce, but the individuals who go into the mining industry go into it with a view to getting large rewards. If they are going to get large rewards they should be prepared to take a commensurate risk.
There is not one in a thousand that makes anything.
That is all very well, but during the past few years, from what I have been able to see, persons engaged in mining have done pretty well.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You have not heard about the losses.

That is just like the old story about the widow and the orphans, always a loss but never a gain. The industries that are receiving this concession, mining and so on, bring about a terrific depletion of Canada's natural resources. Once these resources have been taken out of the ground, they are gone completely. Very often we find the people who have benefited from this kind of operation have no interest in Canada except the amount they can take out of Canada somewhere else.
Oh, oh.

That is perfectly true. How about Sir Harry Oakes? How about Sir

Income War Tax
Herbert Holt? How about a number of others I could mention? What interest had they in Canada except to take everything they could out of the country and go somewhere where they could get tax exemption and would have to pay no succession duties?
Only one or two people have done that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That may apply to Sir Harry Oakes, but it did not apply to Sir Herbert Holt. I am told by the deputy minister that it did not apply to Sir Harry Oakes either.

Leave Sir Harry Oakes out of it entirely. The fact remains that these natural resources belong to the people of Canada. These persons are going to take those resources and use them for their own profit.
They put in more than they take out.

Do not tell me a story like that, that they put in more than they take out. The statement is an obvious absurdity. Many people are trying to get into the mining industry to-day. So far as I am concerned, I am opposed to this concession being made. Once the resources are taken out, there is nothing left but a hole in the ground, except that frequently there is also a ghost town. In many cases the workers who have done the work in the mining industry have had to leave and take a loss on the homes which they have built. Ghost towns dot many parts of this country, and these have been created by mining and other industries of that description which have squandered the natural resources of the country by private exploitation. I am just saying that I am opposed to this legislation.

While the hon. member was speaking, I picked up a paper which contained an interesting Canadian Press dispatch under date of July 27, from Moose Jaw. This reads:
Resources minister J. L. Phelps of Saskatchewan yesterday told delegates to the C.C.P. provincial convention here that the Saskatchewan government is permitting private enterprise to develop northern oil resources because it does not feel ready to take the step itself. He said that the "government will move" at the proper time.
The statement came at the closing session of the three-day convention when P. G. Makaroif of Saskatoon C.C.F. provincial council member, asked why a socialist government was permitting private enternrise to develop oil resources in Saskatchewan and to sell stock.
The two cases are not analogous. In the first instance, the Saskatchewan government will get a royalty from the oil taken out of the ground.
That is all right, is it?

In the second instance, we are proposing as a federal parliament to give complete exemption to the mining industry for three years. Those are two entirely different propositions. We are not opposed to private enterprise, but we demand that private enterprise shall take the risks if it takes the rewards. That is the point. Otherwise it is no longer private enterprise. But what you are trying to do is to remove the risk from private enterprise and to place upon the people of Canada the risks that private enterprise should assume if it is to take the profits for itself.

While I realize that this resolution does not deal with oil and with what took place at the C.C.F. convention in Moose Jaw recently, I want to advise the hon. member for Macleod that, as usual, that press statement carried only half the story. I shall not take time to tell the whole story now.

I should like to make one or two comments on what was said, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I quite agree that we should not take all the risk out of private enterprise, and if he will take the record of what happens in these various mines he will see that there is quite enough risk and loss left even if a certain concession is made at the outset. Before he commits himself against, these alleviations granted to the mining industry, he might take into account one thing he did not mention. He talked of one or two or three people making a lot of money and then leaving the country, and when they do that my feeling? are about the same as his. But he forgot to mention the people who do not make any money. He also forgot to mention another important factor, and that is the amount of labour that goes into these things, which is paid for before anybody makes a nickel out of the mines. He also forgot to mention that we have reasonably efficient income tax laws which take a very large amount of money away from the very few individuals who, after taking the risks, make a little money. Therefore I suggest that his speech was based o,n unsound premises.

The hon member for Rosetown-Biggar introduced the matter of exploration for oil in this country, and he made some disparaging remarks about the terrific waste which had gone on in Alberta and which was going on there now, he said. His remarks indicated a deplorable lack of knowledge of the history of the search for oil
Income War Tax

in Alberta and a lack of understanding of the oil situation as it exists at the present time. There is no tremendous amount of waste of gas going on in Alberta, particularly in the Turner valley, now and has not been for many years.
For how many?
For a number of years. I would not be prepared to say just how many, but conservation measures have been taken there for at least the past ten years.
After twenty-five years of waste.

The hon. member's
statement was as to what was going on now. Following that up, I might point out to the hon. member that had what he thinks should have been done been done, if the oil wells drilled in Turner valley when the field was entirely a wet gas producer had been capped, we would have produced no oil in that country whatever, and the result would have been that the taxpayers of this dominion would have been called upon to pay a bill of some $7,000,000 more in subsidies last year for the prairie provinces alone, let alone the tremendous value that has come from the development of oil in that province. Furthermore, he seems to think that all a man has to do is to drill a mine or an oil well and reap a fortune. Over 8150,000,000 of risk capital has been put up to drill oil wells in Alberta and up to date there have been returns of less than $130,000,000. There have been losses of between $20,000,000 and $25,000,000 to the enterprisers who put up the money to bring oil into production. Possibly he thinks it would have been an excellent thing for the Alberta government or the dominion government to do this oil exploration under government ownership and take that loss. My answer is that they never would have done so and there would have been no oil development if it had been left to governments. Unless private enterprise is given encouragement through proper taxation to go ahead and develop the industry, it will not develop.

This resolution contains what I was trying to secure under resolution 16. In other words, the tax exemption applies to mines that have come into production during the period commencing January 1, 1944, and ending December 31, 1949, which means that a mine coming into operation in 1944, 1945 or 1946 will have a three-year exemption. That privilege is not extended in the case of the cooperatives. I withdrew my amendment at that time because I felt that the minister had given us an undertaking that

he would give the matter consideration. I am pointing this out as a further argument to those I used on resolution 16. In the case of these mines there is an exemption granted which may be considered as being retroactive. The minister made quite a case by saying that we should legislate for 1947 and subsequent years, but in this case we are legislating for as far back as 1944. I am not asking for special privileges but for something along this line under resolution 16.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer to that is that paragraphs (a) and (b) of this resolution simply carry forward an existing exemption which these companies had from excess profits tax in connection with mines which came into production after January, 1944. We are simply continuing that exemption from the excess profits tax.

I do not know that we understand each other. All I am asking is that the same consideration be given to existing cooperatives which started this year or in 1945 or 1944. I think the cases are parallel.
I was interested in hearing, as I always am, what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario had to say. He said that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did not mention the part that labour played in the development of mines. I do not think he was quite correct, because my leader did make reference to the fact that it was the labourer who produced the wealth which he does not always share. If this exemption from income tax also included the man who works in the mines for the first three years, it would have my support.
I would remind the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that to keep one man working underground in the mines in southern Canada eight men are employed outside the mine.

I was interested in hearing the leader of the C.C.F. say that more money was taken out of the mines than was ever piri into them. That statement of his seemed to draw a lot of support from his followers. I am glad that he has such an optimistic impression of the mining industry, particularly the gold-mining industry. I hope, on behalf of himself and his followers, that his optimism is born of personal experience, because so far as gold-mining is concerned it is much too rich for my blood. It is too risky an enterprise, and I mil leave it to younger and more enterprising individuals.
Why look at me?

I should be interested if the hon. member who is the leader of the

Income War Tax
C.C.F. has any figures to demonstrate that far more has been taken out of the ground than has been put into it. I well recall Mark Twain's definition of a mine, "A hole in the ground in which fools throw their money." However, the hon. member may have figures for us. But I think the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar's quarrel is not with lack of enterprise on the part of private individuals, but with the niggardliness of mother nature, who saw fit to deposit gold in very small quantities in, very few places in the world. I not only support the recommendation of the government to grant some tax exemption to these new mines which are now being drilled and which are expected to come in, but I also support the admirable recommendation of my colleague the hon. member for York West for further relief. I do that because I recognize, and if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will be practical and forget his theory he will see, if he has taken the trouble to acquire any knowledge of the facts which now face us, that there is a whole field of gold-bearing rock structure, particularly in the province of Quebec, which is not commercial ore except with the ten per cent premium which golds formerly commanded in terms of Canadian currency, namely $38.50 per ounce as against $35; and if the premium is not available, as is the case to-day, a great many mines which were scheduled to go into production will not be in conjunction with that of his colleague, the able to do so.
It is not a question of whether there is sufficient venturesome money around; it is simply a question of looking at the assay values of the gold-bearing rock and knowing that it is going to turn out so much per ton. It is perfectly foolish to continue to develop that property if you are not going to get back a dollar for the dollar you put in. There must be at least an honest return in that way: other-wish we would be wasting the assets of the country.
The government now sees fit to give these mines on the borderline-and it may apply to the occasional rich mine; I do not know, but the great problem in Canada to-day is the majority of new mines in the Quebec mining area, which badly need it-this alleviation from taxation which the Minister has indicated in the present resolution. However, I should also like to endorse as strongly as I can the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for York West, and say that much of this advantage which the government proposes in the resolution will be lost because the new mines will have a substantial proportion of their pre-development costs and of their mine structural costs-I am not famibar with the exact
terminology of the mining industry-written off compulsorily when they are supposed to be getting three years relief, and perhaps when they have not even profits of any sort from their operations against which to write off the depreciation and depletion costs. In those circumstances, I believe the resolution of the minister is certainly abortive and is nullified by the working of the Department of National Revenue. I hope that the minister's department, Minister of National Revenue, will take these two considerations under advisement, in the interest of these marginal mines, which will either pass out of the picture, or will live, because some relief is given to them, in hope of better times to come. There will then be a chance for this large mining field in Canada to continue to operate.

There is one thought I should like to leave with the acting minister about the remarks which were made by the leader of the C.C.F., the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I do not question for a minute that he was sincere in what he said, but the unfortunate result of a speech like that is this, that when the Department of Finance comes to consider assistance for mines in the years that lie ahead, or even in this session, the thought is apt to arise at once, "Oh, well, some of the members of the house are against any help being given; they think the miners are all big fellows and should not get any help; we had better just go slow about giving this relief. The whole of the C.C.F. are against it. We had better let it ride for another year." The result may very well be that relief will not be given that should be given.
The remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. stem, I am afraid, from the fact that he does not know anything about mining. He comes from a wheat-growing province, Saskatchewan, and his remarks are entirely out of line with the needs of British Columbia. My province is a great mining province. I think that, next to lumbering, mining is our most important industry. I was born in a mining town and raised in a mining district. It was not a case of half a dozen men coming in and making a lot of money and then getting out; everybody in the whole district was interested in mining; nearly everybody had a claim and expected at some time to make forty, fifty, a hundred thousand dollars or perhaps a million. Storekeepers financed prospectors, and many of the prospectors made good. From my own experience, these prospectors were the backbone of that district. Prospectors have opened up large parts of British Columbia; they have made a great contribution to that province. The unfortunate position to-
Income War Tax

day is that the prospectors are practically all gone. And here we have the leader of the C.C.F. rising in his place to-night and conn-plaining about help being given to prospectors.
Prospecting.

Oh, well, "prospecting".
Prospecting is done by individual prospectors. Somebody has to put a pack on his back, go out in the hills and try to find a new mine. Very few new mines are being found in Canada. That is the alarming fact in connection with our mining industry. So I say to the minister, don't just be led up the garden path-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, I won't.
-by the leader of the C.C.F.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not by the C.C.F. My hon. friend may rest assured that we shall be on our guard.
The relief given in this resolution is needed. It will be of help to the mining industry and that industry deserves all the help it can get.
I hesitate about taking part in a discussion of this kind when there are so many experts.
Oh, not that business again!
I was not referring-
Every time you rise you take that line.

I was not referring to the hon. member for Wentworth. There is something strange in the arguments which I heard to-night. If I understand aright what was said, no one makes money in mining; everyone who goes into it takes a loss. That is the argument.
No.
That is the argument that was made-that there was more money put in than was ever taken out.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The argument is that more people are losing than are gaining.
That is right-that there was more money put in mines than was taken out.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Not money; more people lose.
I asked you to prove the contrary; that is all.

I took down the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale. He said it would be perfectly foolish to go on if we 
did not get a dollar back for every dollar we put in. Surely it wrould be perfectly foolish, and soon even my hon. friends, who are so enterprising that they are willing to venture everything, would not carry on very long. It would be foolish even if we got a dollar in return for every dollar invested or ventured. Consequently somebody must be getting more than a dollar's return for every dollar that goes in. But what is happening in this country is that people who cannot afford it are putting money into mines.
What about the horse races?

If the hon. gentleman wishes to play the horses, that is his business. I did not know that was a particularly good business, and I am interested in good business. The people who buy mining stock, the great majority of those who put their money into mines, do not derive the benefits from it. The big fellows do not lose, and if you observe what is going on in Ontario to-day under the security commissioner-I believe that is his title-you will find that many of these men are being prosecuted for fleecing innocent people in this sort of thing.
I am not opposed to the principle of what is proposed here, but it should be done properly. The minerals of Canada are the property of the people of Canada. They are a Canadian asset. A mine is different from a forest or a river or the sea from which we get our fish. Once you have taken the mineral out of the mine there is nothing left.
You could take all the fish out.

No. There would still be suckers left no matter what you did. What should be done-and some government, some day before the mines are depleted will do it, I hope-is to see that the people of Canada as a whole, and not only those who put money into mines shall derive some advantage from these national assets. The miners themselves have an interest in them. What has happened? The member for Vancouver South said that he was brought up in a mining town, but there is not much mining there now'. There are heaps of slag and holes in the ground and lots of dead towns in British Columbia all over the province.
Oh, no; they are not all over the province.

They are all over the province except that part of the province that is not habitable. I have gone all over the province and I know what it is like. What happens is this. The mines are worked out,

Income War Tax
and the people who have settled in those localities find themselves without means to make a living. The result is that they have to move and start life anew somewhere else. What a responsible government should do is to take a part of the profits of the mine and a part of the proceeds of taxation that is levied on the mines and set up a fund, so that when a particular area is worked out the workers who have made their homes there can be removed to new areas where new work is starting up.
Besides that, there is, around these mines, land that can be used for other purposes. There are some agricultural lands that could be developed at the same time. Nothing is done, however, except to take out everything that is in the ground and then to clear out. That is pretty much the case so far as the forests of British Columbia are concerned. It is only within the last few years that, after great pressure, sometimes from the government's forest service employees, who each year drew attention to what was happening to the resources of the province, some action has been taken. Whether it is soon enough to catch up with the spoliation of our resources is a question which no one can answer at the present time. This sort of thing, done in a hit-or-miss fashion to help a few speculators, is not good enough. We should have a programme extended over a number of years that would be beneficial not only to those who are getting money, by hook or by crook, from people who are so innocent that they will put their money on the horses or in a mine-
Or even on the C.C.F.

Oh, no. These people do not put money on the C.C.F. Those who put money on the C.C.F. are people with intelligence who want something for the future. Some day they will get a return, and it will not be a depleted mine.

The hon. member for Vancouver East made a remark to the effect that I was not expert in anjdhing. Let me assure him that I have never posed as an *xpert in anything, but I will say this. Those hon. gentlemen who sit directly to my left profess to be experts on everything under the sun, but I would remind them that those who live in glass houses should be the last to throw stones.

I have lived in a mining district for the past thirty-five years and have seen prospectors going out prospecting. I knew Sir Harry Oakes when he was a poor man like the rest of us in that part of the country, and I know he was one of the best 63260-259
prospectors we had. I do not, therefore, like to hear anyone say things about a man who has gone. I have no brief for him in having left the country, but I can say that there was no finer man than he when he was plain Harry Oakes.
In my opinion, we would not have had a mine in Cobalt or Noranda, or Kirkland Lake or Timmins if any government had been developing those properties, let alone my hon. friends opposite who profess to know so much about mines. I have seen men, prospectors, leaving and staying away for six weeks at a time, and when a prospector comes back one would hardly know that it was the same man. That was the effect that his sojourn in the bush had had upon him.
Of course there is the motivating idea of making money. That was the idea that I had when I first went to that part of the country. I went into lumbering and 'remained in it until I went to Kirkland Lake and got into transportation. I put up the first building in Cobalt and I know what these mining men went through. I should like my hon. friends to start mining, going into a place and spending thousands of dollars in a hole and not getting a cent out of it. See how- long they would stay in power under those conditions.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Timiskaming on what he has said. He has shown something of the pioneering spirit that has made this country what it is to-day, and it is to be devoutly hoped that that spirit will not be killed in this chamber.
I wish to put on the record some figures in answer to the contention that labour and other people in general get no benefits out of mines. The figures I am going to put on the record will show that labour and the town do profit from the mines. In the first place, there is an entirely - wrong impression about the development of mining. A ton of rock is absolutely of no value to the country unless it is developed. If it is developed it is worth to the country in new wealth the minerals it contains.
Briefly, I should like to put these figures on the record, because I think they are germane to the argument we have had to-night. These are the official figures compiled by the department of mines of Quebec for all the mines in western Quebec for 1944. The average value of a ton of ore was $6.35. This was at $38.50 an ounce for gold. The cost of developing was as follows: general development, 57 cents; development, 74 cents; mining, $2.32, and milling, 93 cents, making a total of $4.56 for direct mining costs. That figure of $4.56

Income War Tax

represents very largely the cost of labour. Therefore, out of the $6.35, labour got the bulk of the $4.56 which went for direct mining and milling costs.
Let us get down to cases. Let us look at the profit which all these mines made. The earned surplus of all these mines after taxation was sixty-two cents a ton. The country was better off to the extent of $6.35. Labour got $4.56, or very nearly $4.56. The cost of steel and powder and other things are there, but the great bulk of the cost of mining and milling is labour. Therefore labour got many, many times more out of the $6.35 than did the owners of the property. Surely it is of tremendous advantage to this country that this sort of thing should go on. It is of advantage to labour, because labour gets the bulk of the value of the ore. It is of advantage to the country, because the country is $6.35 richer for every ton of ore that is treated, and there are a great many other advantages as well.
I merely wish to refute as definitely as I can that it is the rich man and the rich company that make the profit. The cost of mining was $4.56, and the profit, sixty-two cents. These are the figures and I think they should be on the record in this debate. That was at $38.50 an ounce for gold.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: With respect to resolutions 31 to 35 inclusive, the tax credits now granted to petroleum, natural gas and mining industries, in respect of exploration expenses are continued for another year with an appropriate adjustment in the reduction of the flat rate tax on corporation income from forts' per cent to thirty per cent. Also under resolution 31, the existing tax credit granted for expenditures in regard to a new oil well is extended to include expenditures incurred in the deepening of an existing well.

In connection with resolutions 31, 32, 33 and 35, which are the ones which deal with oil, gas drilling and exploration. I do not wish to repeat what I said in the budget debate, with reference to these matters. However, I should like to draw to

the minister's attention the five suggestions which I made at that time and to ask him what action the government is prepared to take in connection with them.
So far as the oil industry is concerned, I have been cheered by some of the concessions which the minister has made to the cooperatives and to the mining business since the budget resolutions have been discussed. I was particularly interested in his announcement that, so far as the gold mines were concerned, the depletion allowance was to be changed so that, as he said, those who need help least will not get most. I strongly recommend to him that he change the regulations so far as the depletion allowance for oil wells is concerned, with that same idea in mind.
The other concession given to gold mines is that new mines would pay no income tax for the first two years of operation. In a modified form that might very well be applied to the oil business. As the minister has said earlier this evening, the first three years of an oil well's operations are its most profitable ones. That is quite true; nevertheless a concession which will accomplish much the same effect should be given to oil wells to encourage further drilling.
The five suggestions which I made when I spoke in the budget debate were as follows: First, the extension of the fifty per cent tax drawback for deep-test wells, to completing abandoned exploratory wells. Whether that is covered in the present regulations, I do not know. I hope the minister will clarify that and afford the extension of that fifty per cent drawback to wells drilled in the plains areas, where it is practically essential to have a large amount of drilling if we are to keep up our present oil production in Canada, let alone expand it. Second, an increase in the depletion allowance from the present 33J per cent to 50 per cent, with probably a regulation in connection with it similar to the one they have in the United States, so that it can be spread over several years and carried forward or backward as desired in order to take care of years in which there is no profit, and other years in which there might be a big one. Third, that all drilling costs, permit and leasing expenses, geological and geophysical expenses and so forth be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes and that these deductions be taken as and when desired. That is, they may be carried forward or backward. Fourth, that the present income tax regulations in connection with oil and gas wells be made part of the permanent tax structure in order that operators may be able to make future financial plans knowing where they stand. Fifth, removal of the subsidies now being paid on

Farm Implements
crude oil being imported into the prairie prov-vinces in order to enable western crude oil to reach its true economic level. If the minister would make a statement covering these points we might have a good basis on which to proceed.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.
